FinanceTab.title: Why should I care if share prices fall?
FinanceTab.text:
Major tech firms have seen their stock values fall after a sell-off by investors following the US midterm elections.

The fall in the value of their shares across the world has been blamed on an expectation of a slowdown in AI development, although it comes after sharp rises over recent years.

As companies grow, they may issue shares. Many of the largest companies in the UK have shares which are bought and sold on the London Stock Exchange.

Their collective performance is often quoted amid a blizzard of numbers that may feel confusing and irrelevant.

Booms or falls in the stock market make the news, but rarely does anyone mention the FTSE 100 during a coffee with friends.

Yet, there are good reasons why this performance affects your life and finances.

Many people's initial reaction to "the markets" is that they are not directly affected, because they do not invest money.

Yet there are millions of people with a pension - either private or through work - who will see their savings (in what is known as a defined contribution pension) invested by pension schemes. The value of their savings pot is influenced by the performance of these investments.

Pension savers mostly let experts choose where to invest this money to help it grow. Widespread falls in share prices are likely to be bad news for pension savers.

Hundreds of billions of pounds are held in defined contribution pensions at the moment.

So big rises or falls can affect your pension, but the advice is to remember that pension savings, like any investments, are usually a long-term bet.

Experts say that investors have always had to ride economic shocks. Investments, by definition, require a long-term outlook and strategy. So, they are urging people not to panic in such circumstances or make knee-jerk decisions.

Some people have a pension which promises a specific value, depending on their salary. Others have no pension at all.

Millions of people have been automatically enrolled into a pension and may have not really noticed. Those schemes see employers divert wages into a pension and contribute some money themselves. The government adds a little in tax relief.

In every case, the value of these pension savings is affected by investment performance. So "the markets" matter - maybe not as much as everyday wages, but for future pensions.

Timing is more critical for those at retirement age, as this may be when a retiree uses their pension pot to buy a retirement income, or annuity. The bigger the pot, the more income they will get in retirement.

As you approach retirement age, pension pots tend to be moved to less risky investments, such as government bonds. When stock markets fall, these bonds can do better.

Anyone who has a pension pot invested and is taking an income from it will again see their investment go up and down with the stock markets.

That could mean getting less than you expected if you cash in too much after stock markets have fallen, making it important to plan how to make up any of this shortfall, experts say.

However, higher interest rates tend to mean better rates offered on annuities, and there is a chance of more rate rises in the UK by the Bank of England.

If share prices fall for an extended period then that could have an effect on jobs.

That's because investors in the company expect a return on that investment.

When it falls for a while, then they would expect the business to address issues, for example by cutting costs, and therefore jobs.

There is a huge element of the unknown here though. Companies have to consider lots of factors when making decisions on investment and employment.

In purely investment terms, lower share prices can offer an opportunity to buy, in the hope that over the long term, they recover and rise. Many people will do this initially through a stocks and shares Individual Savings Account (Isa).

However, it is worth noting that the sell-off in tech stocks in particular came after big rises, so long-term investors are still likely to have seen gains.

Experts and regulators are at pains to point out that investments can go down as well as up, and urge people not to put everything into one investment, but to diversify.

Some people invest money in what are known as tracker funds. These go up and down in line with the performance of a certain index, such as the FTSE 100.

So if the index falls, so does the value of their investments and vice versa. One advantage of these funds is that they often cost relatively little to sign up to.

When we see big shifts in the stock markets there can also be fluctuations in the value of currencies and exchange rates.

As a result, prices could go up, but could also go down.

Upheaval to economies across the world, to oil prices and so on, have a big impact on what we pay at home for goods and services, so there are lots of factors in play.

FinanceTab.title: Why smoky bacon crisps threaten to reignite rows over EU rules
FinanceTab.text:
The naming of smoky bacon-flavoured crisps has become the latest political headache to emerge from the government's bid for closer ties with the EU.

The government is negotiating a deal on food standards in a bid to cut costs for British companies trading with Europe.

Labour ministers have been keen to talk up the potential economic benefits of the agreement, which could be announced at a summit later this month.

But the deal's requirement for Britain to adopt EU food rules in a wide range of areas has threatened to reignite sovereignty debates from the Brexit era.

Labour ministers have been keen to sidestep talking about the impact of alignment in particular sectors, instead stressing the overall economic boost it expects the food deal to bring.

On Thursday, Environment Secretary Angela Eagle told a radio presenter he should "get a life" when he asked about the potential impact of the new rules on snacks, such as smoky bacon crisps.

But it highlights the political dangers for the government of realigning with regulations that British politicians have not been able to shape, with the Conservatives and Reform UK keen to pounce on cases showing Britain to be a "rule taker" from Brussels.

It is not the first regulatory skirmish over smoky bacon crisps - following previous headlines over how the well-loved British flavour could be affected by an EU decision in 2024 to phase out a number of artificial smoke flavourings.

Now, the flavour name itself has been called into question by a separate EU attempt to restrict how descriptions of meat are used to market food.

Under rules adopted this summer, the EU plans to restrict the use of 31 terms, including bacon, drumstick and steak, to products that contain meat, claiming consumers could be confused by plant-based alternatives using the same names.

The European snack industry is seeking clarity on how the rules, which will also cover terms such as pork, chicken and beef, would apply to meat-flavoured crisps, including those flavoured without the use of any meat extracts.

The UK government has said it expects the new regulations to be in scope of its proposed food standards deal.

This means they would also apply to companies marketing their products in Britain, which is among the biggest consumers of crisps in Europe, according to analysts Euromonitor., external

It has raised the prospect that crisps with names such as smoky bacon and roast chicken could have to be relabelled to be sold in British shops, although much remains unclear about how the rules will apply in practice.

The new EU rules, which will not come into force until after August 2029, will allow the European Commission to create exemptions for meaty names with an established long-term use to describe other types of food product.

The Brussels-based body is yet to set out how it plans to use this power, or what it means for snacks.

A group of conservative German MEPs are also seeking a specific carve-out for meat names in snacks and sauces in separate legislation, external currently making its way through the European Parliament.

The Food and Drink Federation, which represents British crispmakers including Walkers and KP Snacks, has been supportive of the government's bid to reach a food deal due to its potential to reduce trade barriers with Europe.

But it has highlighted the new rules as an example of where it wants the government to work with industry to ensure UK interests are reflected in EU decision making.

"Meat protections are an example of a new EU rule that UK businesses will need to comply with, but which the UK was not involved in developing," added the body's chief scientific officer Kate Halliwell.

FinanceTab.title: Andy Burnham tells firms to publish salaries in job adverts ahead of new law
FinanceTab.text:
Businesses should publish salaries in job adverts now, Prime Minister Andy Burnham is telling firms, rather than wait for a new law to come in that will force them to do so.

The government is planning to make pay details compulsory in adverts, with legislation on the issue being brought forward "as soon as possible".

It argues the change will help jobseekers, particularly those applying for their first job, and could help prevent pay discrimination. However, one industry group said setting pay was a complex process and regulating adverts was not always suitable.

It comes a week after the UK's equality watchdog said employees should legally be able to find out what their colleagues are earning.

Burnham said the current system felt "weighted against the applicant" and the changes were aimed at "tilting the scales back".

"It can be quite soul destroying for young people these days, applying for jobs when the salary is not listed but sometimes they're not getting a reply," he told the BBC.

The prime minister added that publishing salaries in adverts was also important for closing the gender pay gap.

He was also challenged over whether MPs should be disclosing salaries when advertising for staff in their offices.

A number of politicians are currently advertising for roles without giving an expected salary., external

Burnham said: "It would apply completely to them too and the call I'm making today is, before the law changes do it voluntarily because it's the right thing to do."

The Cabinet Office launched a consultation into pay and reducing discrimination in the summer, and the government said there had been "overwhelming support" for greater transparency, with 94% of respondents backing the move.

"Whether you're a young person starting out or a parent trying to support your family, you should know what a job pays before spending your time and effort applying for it," Burnham said.

The government said the move was part of attempts to reduce the nearly one million young people not in education, employment or training - or "Neet" - ahead of the final report of the Milburn Review into youth inactivity, which is due in the coming weeks.

Publishing salary details upfront could "expose unjustified differences in pay, give workers greater confidence to challenge discrimination and prevent disagreements over pay escalating into disputes".

The proposals are similar to measures being introduced in the European Union., external

Employers in Europe will have to disclose the initial pay or range for new roles, which must either be included in a published job advert or shared before an interview.

According to data from UK jobs website Adzuna, external, 51% of the adverts on its site in September had salary information, but the proportion has been falling in recent years.

Adzuna co-founder Andrew Hunter said being open about pay "should be the norm, not the exception".

He added that employers who put a salary on a job advert "attract more applicants, and better-suited ones".

Previous research from the CIPD, external, an industry body for human resources managers, has indicated that the public sector and charities are more likely to reveal pay information that private firms, while pay ranges were more common than specific salaries.

But it found not all employers were "fully transparent", with pay ranges sometimes wider than £10,000.

CIPD chief executive Neil Carberry said that while, in principle, giving salary details was "a good thing", in practice it was "more complicated".

"There isn't always a single fixed figure, and employers will want to set pay based on a candidate's skills, experience and potential."

Carberry added the process was complex, saying that drafting job adverts is "best left to good employer practice rather than government regulation".

The government has said it will set out further details on what information will be required and how the legislation will be enforced "in due course".

Conservative shadow business secretary Julia Lopez said: "At a time when employers are finding it harder and harder to take on staff, Labour have decided to make their lives even more difficult.

"It should be up to businesses to decide what information they advertise about job openings, and to decide how to attract the best applicants.

"As long as they are not being dishonest, misleading or discriminatory, it should not be a matter for the government."

Last week, the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC), said publishing salaries in job adverts would be a "positive step".

It also said bosses should be required to respond to questionnaires about colleagues' pay to cut pay discrimination.

At present, employers do not have to respond to employee requests for salary information about their co-workers.

The EHRC also said employers should be prevented from asking about current salary when offering a job to stop a history of discrimination from continuing.

Employers in the UK are currently allowed to ask you how much you get paid in your current role, but applicants are under no obligation to tell them.

FinanceTab.title: 'I was asked if I was a crier': Your worst job interviews revealed
FinanceTab.text:
Tiara Allen arrived on time to interview for a retail job. Her interviewer didn't.

She waited for around 40 minutes in a shopping centre while the interviewer's co-worker called them "two or three times".

When they finally showed up, Tiara says she was told it was because the meeting wasn't in the schedule.

She needed work at the time, so took the job when she was offered it, but says she would handle the situation differently now.

"I would not take a job if they took that long," she says, adding that she believed her treatment during the interview was a sign of how the firm tended to treat staff.

Tiara is far from alone. She is one of many people who spoke to the BBC about their worst job interview experiences after we wrote about the one interview question that leaves you feeling uncomfortable.

While those situations can be hard to deal with in the moment, they can also teach us a lot about the world of work.

During an interview for an assistant at a book publisher in New York, Chas Edwards was asked a question he wasn't expecting.

"I was asked for my first job if I was a crier," he recalls.

Thinking the interviewer was being funny, Chas replied that he didn't cry. He was later told that this was why he got the job.

"Her last assistant had cried – too often, I guess? – and she wanted someone who didn't cry. So she was being serious and I thought it was a joke," he says.

It was a bad sign. Chas says it was "a terrible, terrible job with a miserable boss" and while he managed to make it through 13 months there without crying he was "crying inside".

"I set the world record for working for this person. No-one had ever lasted three months with her before," he recalls.

Despite all this, Chas says he is in some ways grateful the experience was so awful.

"Because every job since then, even the bad ones, are not that bad," he says, adding that he can "cry anywhere now".

Corinne Card also found herself floored when the first question she was asked in an interview for an administrative job was if she liked working with people.

When she replied yes, she was told that the job wouldn't be for her and the interview ended there.

"I don't know if it was a deliberate trap. Because who would answer 'I don't like working with people'?"

Corinne Mills, joint managing director of Personal Career Management, says that it can be worth asking an interviewer to clarify any weird questions, perhaps by repeating the question back to them.

However, if a line of questioning is really off-putting, she says it can also be a sign of what it's like to work there, saying that interviews are also about candidates judging the company.

Meanwhile, other questions are not just annoying – they are illegal.

Discrimination against a protected characteristic is against the law, external, meaning an employer cannot treat you less favourably based on your age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage, pregnancy, race, religion, sex, or sexual orientation.

Employment lawyer Roy Magara says that women being asked if they intend on having children in an interview is a "quite common" kind of bias. He says he has also seen a case where an older candidate was told he didn't get the job after an interview because he didn't fit the "vibe" of a younger team.

If you think these sorts of biases took place in your interview, Roy says you can send the company a subject access request, external to see how they discussed your application internally.

Worst-case scenarios like these can make interviews feel very difficult, especially considering the control employers have over candidates.

Euan Cameron, co-founder of hiring software Willo, says that even with this power imbalance it's important not to overthink what an interview is.

"An interview is just a conversation between two people," he says.

Of course, as in Tiara's case, it helps when both of those people show up.

FinanceTab.title: Interest rates hiked to 4% in first increase in over three years
FinanceTab.text:
Interest rates have risen for the first time in more than three years and the Bank of England has signalled a further increase is likely unless the US-Iran war is resolved.

Rates rose to 4% from 3.75% in a bid to curb inflation mainly driven by the conflict's impact on global oil prices.

Andrew Bailey, the Bank's governor, said the decision "shouldn't be seen as the first in an inevitable long sequence of hikes", but warned "unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, neither does it seem likely to be the last increase".

The higher level will increase the cost of borrowing for things such as mortgages, loans and credit cards, but will also lead to higher returns on savings.

The Bank's rate-setting committee all backed increasing interest rates, with eight out of nine voting in favour of the rise to 4%. One member wanted an even bigger increase to 4.25%.

Bailey said the hike was warranted due to higher energy prices and pointed to what happens in the Middle East as the main factor in future decisions.

"Put simply, it requires real progress towards settling the conflict in the Middle East," the governor said.

Bailey said he could "see the argument" for a further rate hike, before taking a "more conditional approach" dependent on the path of energy prices and inflation in the coming months.

However, the views of members on the rate-setting committee differed on the path forward.

Clare Lombardelli agreed there was "likely to be a case for a further increase in rates in the near term", while Megan Greene went further, suggesting "additional hikes" might be likely depending on how inflation impacted wages, prices and the jobs market.

However, Alan Taylor said the rate rise was a "a risk-management 'one-for-now' insurance hike".

Inflation, which measures the pace of price rises over time, is well below its peak of a few years ago but remains above the Bank of England's 2% target and is expected to increase further next year.

Prices rose 3.5% in the year to September 2026, largely due to higher fuel prices. Millions of households are also set to be hit by energy bill increases in January.

Higher fuel prices can lead to prices rising for a host of goods and staples as businesses pass on higher costs to customers.

But the Bank said there was "limited evidence" this had happened so far for goods, such as food, with some firms absorbing cost increases and accepting lower margins.

In an interview with the BBC, Bailey defended the decision to raise rates despite the Bank's assessment that inflation was yet to spread to other parts of the economy.

He said further increases in energy prices are putting upward pressure on inflation and "that's what we have to seek to lean against".

FinanceTab.title: Faisal Islam: How high will interest rates go?
FinanceTab.text:
Interest rates have risen to 4% and the Bank of England has indicated there are more rises to come. The question is how many? There is a split on the rate-setting committee here.

Three of the nine voting members referred to "rises" plural. One member voted for a bigger increase, to 4.25%. Three referred to just one more including governor Andrew Bailey.

My read on this is that the expectation is for one more rise in February. Two and done, but it depends.

It is painful for those on variable mortgages, but should not be seen as the start of a cycle of hikes.

Predicting where interest rates will go is like throwing darts at a board that constantly moves around the wall, with expectations of how long the Iran War will last and its impact on the economy and prices lurching from day to day.

At least there is no blindfold.

The Bank's forecasts indicate inflation is heading to just under 5% next spring as a typical household energy bill surges by 27% in January to £2,150 a year.

Why have they raised now? High and rising inflation risks a further cycle of self fulfilling expectations of rising prices. It hasn't been seen so far, however. The war has lasted for 9 months, and led to oil prices used in the forecast averaging $108 a barrel.

And yet on the day they have announced the rate rise, the oil price is actually 13% lower than that having fallen in the run up and after the US mid term elections, reflecting expectations or guesses that President Trump will now retreat or deescalate from the Iran war.

The other notable factor is that the UK economy is performing much better than forecasts and expectations. This is underlined by the Bank of England's latest forecasts.

Growth has been 0.6%, and 0.5% in the first two quarters of the year. It is heading for 0.7%, the Bank said, between July and September, before slowing in the three months to the end of the year. Unemployment has stabilised, actually falling a little.

Some of this has fed through into a better performing currency, with sterling at its highest level since the Brexit referendum, when measured against a basket of currencies. This can help rein in inflation by making imports cheaper.

So, this is an unusual type of uncertainty. Even the expected further rise, probably in February next year is conditional on the war continuing.

The Bank of England stopped waiting for President Trump's war to end today, but perhaps the Democrats' resounding victory in the US midterm elections will stop the inflationary wave? The Bank has thrown a tentative first dart, and there is probably another to come.

FinanceTab.title: Global tech stocks plunge as US midterms add to AI slowdown fears
FinanceTab.text:
Global stock markets have tumbled after investors sold tech shares on fears that the US midterm elections would slow the development of artificial intelligence (AI).

The sell-off, which started in the US and then spread to Asia and Europe, has seen trillions of dollars wiped off the stock value of major tech firms.

In the US, the tech-heavy Nasdaq share index sank 5.5% on Thursday. Asian markets also saw hefty falls on Friday and European markets opened lower.

Investors are worried about tougher regulation of AI, after Democrat candidates opposed the data centres needed by the technology. The share falls also come on top of concerns about whether the huge amounts being spent on AI will pay off.

The sell-off in US stocks meant the so-called magnificent seven tech companies, including Apple, Nvidia and Tesla, shed a trillion dollars in value in a single trading day, with Nvidia shares sliding more than 9%.

Shares in Elon Musk's companies SpaceX and Tesla also plunged, falling 8% and nearly 11% respectively and shaving more than $300bn off the firms' market value.

Musk had spent nearly $450m backing Republican campaigns, including at least $45m in support of Ken Paxton for the Texas senate seat, but Texas turned blue in the Democratic tsunami on Tuesday.

The sharp fall in the Nasdaq meant it lost an estimated $2.5tn (£1.9tn) in market value. The index is now in what market watchers call correction territory, which is where an index or company value falls at least 10% below its recent high.

However, the huge gains seen by tech stocks in recent times - driven by the enthusiasm for AI - mean that even after Thursday's fall, the Nasdaq is still higher than it was a year ago, and up about 4.6% from where it was at the start of this year.

The US sell-off spread into Asia on Friday. The Nikkei share index in Japan closed down 6% as shares in memory chip makers Kioxia and Tokyo Electron saw big falls.

In South Korea, the Kospi index plunged more than 8% at one point, triggering a so-called circuit breaker, a mechanism that temporarily halts trading to curb panic selling.

The Kospi eventually closed down 6%, with shares in chipmaker SK Hynix falling more than 10%.

European markets fell on Friday, although the declines were not as severe as the indexes contain fewer tech stocks. The UK's FTSE 100 index fell nearly 2% while Germany's Dax index was down 2.4%.

Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said investors were worried about the huge amounts of money being spent on AI with "no clear idea of when, or whether, there will be payback".

"The midterm election result muddied the waters as the Democrats now have more influence and could slow down the pace of data centre roll-outs and look at new ways to regulate the sector," he added.

"The AI story has all been about speed, and now there is a danger of it moving to a lower gear, and some of the wheels falling off."

FinanceTab.title: Binance says fake job interviews used as part of $6.3bn crypto hack
FinanceTab.text:
Hackers who stole a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) from Binance used fake job interviews and a compromised internal AI tool, the firm has revealed.

Initial findings published by the company, which operates the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, said hackers gained access to its systems through a "sophisticated, multi-stage campaign".

It said they used a range of techniques such as malicious software downloads to compromise the computers of Binance engineers and gain control over tools to drain its wallet of billions of dollars worth of crypto.

Binance called it a "serious and highly sophisticated security incident" and apologised, saying "this should not have happened".

In a post on X, external, Binance said hackers targeted its engineers using social engineering techniques.

These see hackers use approaches such as phishing to trick people into parting with sensitive or personal details, which can then be used to try and access their accounts.

Binance said as part of the hack, one of its engineers was contacted through a legitimate job-hunting platform and invited to bogus job interviews with fake company representatives.

It said the perpetrators used "more advanced and deceptive" methods to build trust with him, such as sharing social media accounts which contained personal images.

The engineer in question was instructed to download malware masquerading as an "assignment" during a second interview, which deployed malicious code with "obfuscation techniques" evading detection.

Binance said hackers then leveraged the engineer's compromised computer and an internal AI tool to gain control over two other engineers' laptops, and execute the next steps of the attack.

The incident led the firm to suspend withdrawals for customers globally, meaning users could not get their cryptocurrency out of the platform until the service was restored on Sunday.

Customers withdrew billions of dollars worth of assets after it reopened.

"We apologise for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry," it said.

The company added it had taken a range of steps following the incident, including working with law enforcement to trace and freeze affected assets.

It said it had also set aside more than 100% of the funds needed to cover the loss, and said 98% of the token assets impacted had been "replenished" as of Saturday.

FinanceTab.title: Trump may have lost but don’t bet Democrats can fix the economy
FinanceTab.text:
It was the economy, again. Although Donald Trump largely ignored it, voters’ acute concerns over the rising cost of living fuelled a political upheaval for the ages that is likely to deliver the biggest swing toward Democrats since Watergate, granting them the largest House majority in nearly four decades alongside their biggest edge in the Senate since 2008.

Still, having come to power promising to restore affordability, the new crop of Democrats are soon to discover that there is not much they can do over the next couple of years to alleviate angry voters’ stress over pricey gas and groceries, exorbitant mortgages and unaffordable healthcare.

Democrats would do well to recall that the affordability strains that helped deliver them to power are not dissimilar to those that delivered the presidency to Trump two years ago. And they could again quickly become their enemy.

“First, Americans want Washington to bring down the cost of living,” said Chuck Schumer, Senate majority leader-in-waiting. Likely House speaker Hakeem Jeffries added that “we’ve promised to fight for an affordable America, and that’s exactly what we will do”. They will soon discover the limits to their power to undo Trump’s economic blunders and steer an economy that is largely driven by forces outside their control.

Take gas prices, the single most powerful motivation for voters’ rebellion against the Republicans enabling Trump’s policy choices. Reining them in will require reaching an understanding with Iran that reopens the strait of Hormuz. Schumer thinks Democrats can achieve that. “We are going to end the war,” he said.

Trump may disagree, however. And while it is true that Congress is legally entitled to end wars – it is the only branch of government entitled to start one – it is unclear what such legal niceties might mean in practice. Republicans have controlled Congress since Trump went to war. Still, he has pursued it without asking for their approval. Democrats could now try to cut war funding, but they do not have the requisite 60 Senate votes to prevent a filibuster.

Trump’s trade war has similar characteristics. When the supreme court struck down Trump’s “national security” tariffs because they exceeded presidential authority, the administration reimposed many of them under a different statute, deploying a new, also spurious rationale. There is also little that Democrats can do to stop Trump’s war on immigration. It is fully funded and can carry on unimpeded, further disrupting construction and other immigrant-reliant industries.

Even the low-hanging fruit hangs rather high. While it may seem easy to reinstate federal subsidies for health insurance programs under the Affordable Care Act, or undo or postpone cuts to Medicaid and food stamps in Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Democrats will be hard-pressed to find the money, given a budget deficit that is already running at a whopping 6% of the nation’s gross domestic product.

Just preventing further damage will be an uphill battle. A lame duck Trump who no longer feels the need to please voters is likely to give free rein to his most destructive urges. While Democrats will be able to block Trump’s new legislative proposals, they don’t have the votes to overcome presidential vetoes.

Optimists may believe that after Tuesday’s shellacking, sufficient Republicans in Congress could be convinced to buck their president’s wishes. But most of those who survived the bloodbath come from the most faithful Maga districts and states and are the least likely to abandon their leader.

The economy itself – driven almost exclusively by a frenzied artificial intelligence investment boom – is unlikely to help Democrats achieve their goal of easing voters’ economic strains.

Wall Street is already doubting that the massive investments to build data-processing centers to train powerful AI models will pay off in time to justify the money. The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index has fallen by more than 10% in the last month.

Goldman Sachs estimates that the large AI hyperscalers have raised almost $200bn in bond markets so far this year, almost twice as much as in all of 2025. Altogether, the bank added, AI-related firms have raised nearly $500bn in debt so far in 2026.

Were this bubble to pop and the funding to stop, it would likely deliver an economic downfall to beat even the Great Recession sparked by the housing bubble in 2008. When the time comes, a government hamstrung by $40tn in debt and interest rates hovering near 20-year highs will have little fiscal space to soften the blow.

Can voters’ newfound love for Democrats survive the likely turbulence ahead? Justin Wolfers, an economist at the University of Michigan who runs Platypus Economics, observes that neither the unemployment rate nor inflation are bad enough to justify Americans’ extreme pessimism about the economy. So what’s driving the sour mood? A collapse in confidence in economic leadership.

Tuesday’s Republican bloodbath might, on its own, improve Americans’ spirits. Limited though their powers may be, Democrats will at least offer some resistance to Trump’s most destructive impulses. But the economy will likely pose a greater challenge for the new Democratic Congress than it has to the Republicans currently in charge. In two years’ time, Democrats might be facing anger over an economic scenario that has gotten palpably worse.

They might then come to embrace the limits of their power and hope voters blame the president – not Congress – for their economic unhappiness.

FinanceTab.title: US job growth exceeds expectations in October despite economic uncertainty
FinanceTab.text:
The US added 165,000 jobs to the economy in October, a sign of resilience in the labor market amid ongoing war in the Middle East and inflation, according to new data released on Friday.

Economists had said the labor market has been stuck in a “low-hire, low-fire” state, in which job growth is sluggish but layoffs also remain low, but October’s data surpassed economist expectations. The unemployment rate went down slightly to 4.1%, the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reported.

Average hourly earnings increased at an annual rate of 3.1%, slightly higher than last month. Inflation over the last few months has largely outpaced the growth in wages – what often leads people to feel they are spending even more to buy essentials. In September, the annualized inflation rate was 3.7%.

Initial figures for August and September were also revised up by a total of 84,000 jobs. Job growth was seen in healthcare, transportation, warehousing and manufacturing.

Other data released earlier this week showed employment has been steady. Layoffs in September fell to their lowest level in a year and a half, according to the bureau, while outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas tracked just under 44,000 layoffs in October – a 71% decrease compared with last October.

The new data comes after a seismic midterm election that solidified Democrats’ control of Congress for the next two years. Multiple polls had shown Americans were most frustrated about the state of the economy, especially higher gas and grocery prices.

“Americans delivered a clear verdict in the midterm elections that the current economy is squeezing people financially and making it hard to get by, let alone get ahead,” said Heather Long, chief economist at the Navy Federal Credit Union, in a statement before Friday’s report. “The labor market is a good example of why people are frustrated.”

But it’s unclear when Americans will get relief. Gas prices are on average $1 a gallon higher than they were a year ago because of the war in Iran. The price of diesel, which is used throughout the supply chain to power large vehicles, is 60% higher compared with prewar levels.

In times of stubborn inflation, the US Federal Reserve usually intervenes by raising interest rates, which slows price increases. In September, the Fed hiked interest rates for the first time since 2023, bringing them up to a range of 3.75%-4%, citing inflation. Though officials kept rates steady at their last meeting in October, held the week before the election, economists are expecting one more rate hikes at the next central bank meeting in December.

Meanwhile, markets over the last week have been shaken as investors appeared worried about AI spending. After reaching correction territory, when an index drops 10% below its most recent peak, the tech-heavy Nasdaq index briefly made a recovery on Wednesday before diving back into correction territory on Thursday.

SportsTab.title: England 45-22 Australia: Hosts swat aside Wallabies at Twickenham
SportsTab.text:
Tries: George, Chessum, Heyes, Van Poortvliet, Pollock (2), Spencer Cons: F Smith (5)

Tries: Jorgensen, Daugunu, Williams Cons: Lonergan, Donaldson Pens: Lonergan

England provided emphatic on-pitch backing for head coach Steve Borthwick as they scored seven tries to swat aside a listless Australia at Allianz Stadium.

The build-up was marked by questions over England's form, which has been poor for most of 2026, and a reported rift between players and coaches during the summer.

Senior players angrily insisted on Friday the squad and staff were still united, and their performance on Sunday would demonstrate as such.

There are stiffer Tests to come, with New Zealand arriving in a fortnight, but Borthwick sailed through this referendum with flying colours.

His team played with determination and physicality, but also dexterity and ambition, in their most complete display of the year by a long margin.

They were heartily endorsed by the home crowd, who spent the final quarter serenading their side with Swing Low and willing Henry Pollock, brought on to fill in for wing Immanuel Feyi-Waboso, to complete a hat-trick after an enterprising cameo out wide.

Pollock was denied his third, but it was one of the few things his side missed out on during a most satisfying outing.

Borthwick had made a fast start, along with tidying up discipline, a key aim for his side.

They seemed to have delivered on the former inside 120 seconds. After a typically bustling carry from Ben Earl, soft hands from the excellent Seb Atkinson and Fin Smith released Feyi-Waboso on a carving line that took him under the posts.

It was a moment full of the intensity, intention and invention that England are desperate to show.

Unfortunately for the hosts the celebrations were curtailed, with the score chalked off for Ben Curry's pass straying forward to Ollie Chessum in a previous phase.

They didn't have to wait long however.

On eight minutes, Australia's own indiscipline paved the way to the first England try.

After an obstruction as England chased a kick, Smith put his forwards into the corner and their driven maul survived Australia's counter and wound its way over the line, with Jamie George locked on for the score.

A loose and limp Australia provided the perfect backdrop for a statement in the first half.

Feyi-Waboso was the swerving, centre point of England's early endeavour.

After missing the entirety of the Six Nations through injury, the 23-year-old brings electric pace and evasion to the backline.

His break set up a prime position, deep inside Australia's 22m, for England's second try, with Henry Slade and George Furbank's raking miss passes giving Chessum room to canter in.

With Australia prop Angus Bell yellow-carded for a hip-drop tackle on Feyi-Waboso, Joe Heyes splintered off the side of a driven maul to put England 19-3 clear after little more than half an hour.

It was the least their dominance deserved.

However Max Jorgensen's interception on the stroke of half-time, picking off Jack van Poortvliet's pass to race away under the posts, evoked memories of 2024.

In the teams' meeting that year, Australia hung on to the coat-tails of a fast-starting England before Jorgensen scored a last-gasp decisive try to seal the Wallabies' win.

With Feyi-Waboso failing to return after the break, back row Pollock brought off the bench to fill a wing spot in the absence of back-three replacements and their lead only nine, England were not clear of danger.

However a delicious try, created by Furbank's pinpoint incision and deft offload, Freeman's inside pass and scorer Van Poortvliet's support line, restored England's cushion after the restart, in the final play before Bell's return from the sin bin.

A quick-fire double from Pollock extended the hosts' advantage. For his first try he snaffled a loose ball and picked a path to the line, before showing his pace from further out to round off a lovely move featuring Smith, Freeman and Furbank.

Australia were 38-10 down and set to record a losing margin against England, eclipsing the 24 points they were beaten by in 2017 and 2019.

Tries from Filipo Daugunu and Jeremy Williams in the final 20 minutes averted that fate, but there was no disguising the gulf between the teams.

With a home Rugby World Cup to come in less than a year, Wallabies boss Les Kiss, who was visibly angry in the coaches' box, has plenty of work to do.

So does Borthwick, who saw Ben Spencer intercept and dive over for his first Test try to round off victory.

He will have concerns over centre Atkinson, who departed with a painful-looking leg injury in the second half, and Feyi-Waboso, who emerged at full-time in a protective boot.

But the England head coach can advance into autumn in a position of considerably more comfort.

SportsTab.title: Abu Dhabi Championship: Jon Rahm pips Tyrrell Hatton and Rory McIlroy to win on DP World Tour
SportsTab.text:
Abu Dhabi Championship final-round leaderboard

-23 J Rahm (Spa); -21 T Hatton (Eng); -19 R McIlroy (NI); -17 F Laporta (Ita); -16 B Wiesberger (Aut), A Ayora (Spa), D Puig (Spa); -15 J Schaper (SA)

Selected others: -14 N Kimsey (Eng), M Jordan (Eng); -13 S Bairstow (Eng), T Fleetwood (Eng), A Sullivan (Eng); -12 E Ferguson (Sco); -11 E Chacarra (Spa); -10 A Rai (Eng); -9 M Wallace (Eng); -4 P Reed (US)

Jon Rahm fired a final-round 67 to clinch a two-shot victory over England's Tyrrell Hatton at the Abu Dhabi Championship.

It was a first victory for the two-time major winner since he announced his departure from LIV Golf, and a first win at a DP World Tour event in four years.

The Spaniard, in his first tournament since the birth of his fourth child last month, produced six birdies with just one dropped shot on Sunday to finish clear of Hatton with Northern Ireland's Rory McIlroy another two strokes further back.

"It means a lot. It's been quite a while to play well in the DP World Tour," Rahm told Sky Sports.

"Except a shot on 17, as far as I'm concerned, I played a pretty flawless back nine. It was really solid, never in danger of making a bogey except that one hole.

"After everything that has gone on, some poor play and some battles mentally with a lot of noise, to come back out after a bit of a break and a new addition to the family, it's pretty special."

Having finished at the very bottom of the leaderboard at the BMW PGA Championship at Wentworth in his last appearance, Rahm joked that going "last to first" was especially pleasing.

For McIlroy, his third-placed finish was enough to ensure he goes into next week's season-finale at the DP World Tour Championship sitting second in the Race To Dubai standings as he seeks a record-equalling eighth win.

The 37-year-old, who was given a two-shot penalty in his first round, leapfrogged American Patrick Reed and now trails only Spain's Eugenio Chacarra in his bid to match Colin Montgomerie's eight season-long titles.

Despite starting the week outside the top 50, Rahm's victory ensured he remained in the hunt too should he be able to go back-to-back in Dubai.

SportsTab.title: Tromso v Bodo/Glimt: Fan injured after falling through hole in away stand
SportsTab.text:
A fan was taken to hospital after a number of Bodo/Glimt supporters fell through a hole in the away stand at Tromso.

The Norwegian top-flight match at Romssa Arena on Sunday was paused just before half-time after Bodo keeper Nikita Haikin called for the referee's attention.

Bodo/Glimt press officer Simen Pedersen told the Reuters news agency that "up to five people fell through the stands".

"We stood and bounced to a supporter song, then the floor gave way," Bodo supporter Andrine Moen told local newspaper Verdens Gang, as reported by Reuters.

"It cracked in two in the row in front of us. There were at least two people who fell through the floor, but we don't know how far they fell or how many fell in total."

The remaining Bodo supporters were moved into other parts of the ground before the match resumed.

The match at Tromso's stadium - the northernmost venue in Norway's Eliteserien - was played in heavy rain.

The score was 0-0 at the time of the incident, but Bodo forward Ola Brynhildsen scored twice after the game resumed to give the league leaders a 2-0 win.

Bodo are locked in a title battle with Viking and the Eliteserien season is set to finish in the first week of December.

SportsTab.title: Usman Khawaja: I have not thrown anyone under the bus with relevations
SportsTab.text:
Usman Khawaja said he has "not thrown anyone under the bus" with revelations about the sandpaper scandal that engulfed the Australia team in 2018.

In his autobiography - Sabr - and in an interview with the Sydney Morning Herald, Khawaja claimed the entire team should take responsibility for the plot to use sandpaper on the ball in the third Test against South Africa eight years ago.

At the time, the only players punished were captain Steve Smith, vice-captain David Warner and opener Cameron Bancroft.

Speaking in videos posted on Instagram on Sunday to clarify his comments, Khawaja said: "You would have seen when I mentioned it was all of us, that's implying that whether we like it or not, we are all responsible for what happened together.

"As a team, we need to take that collectively. That is all.

"But now that everyone's talking, am I going to deny that everyone knew? Nah, I won't deny that, either. But I never speak on behalf of anyone else in my book, contrary to what the headlines in clickbait media would have you think."

Other players involved in the Cape Town controversy have repeatedly denied involvement or knowledge of the plot to alter the condition of the ball by rubbing it with sandpaper.

Four bowlers who played for Australia in that Test - Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon - remain part of the team. Cummins has been Test captain since 2021.

In 2021, the quartet released a joint statement which said they "did not know a foreign substance was taken on to the field".

On Saturday, Darren Lehmann, the Australia coach who resigned in the wake of the ball-tampering scandal, also denied Khawaja's claims when he told ABC: "I don't think everyone would have known."

Khawaja retired from international cricket in January. He scored 6,229 runs in 88 Tests for Australia.

In October, it was revealed that Khawaja had met with Cummins to discuss the contents of the upcoming autobiography.

That meeting took place before Australia's recent Test series in South Africa, which the Proteas won 2-1.

In the videos on Instagram, 39-year-old Khawaja explained that blame for the plot should have been shared among the entire set-up, not only Smith, Warner and Bancroft.

"I waited till the [South Africa] series was over. And you know what? I haven't thrown anyone under the bus," Khawaja said.

"The guys that are currently in the team right now and the other people that were there on the South African tour, including me, we're not the victims.

"These three guys took the blame for all of us, and they're the victims. Yes, it was tough for everyone, including me. I had sleepless nights, too."

Khawaja also defended not revealing his version of the sandpaper saga at the time, or following the bowlers' statement in 2021, and instead waiting for his autobiography.

"You ask why didn't I say anything in those four years after that while I was still playing? You know what? I never wanted to be the first guy to chat about this," he said.

"Call me a chicken or whatever you want, I didn't know how to do it because I was still on the team. How was I ever supposed to bring this up when I knew some of my team-mates didn't want to talk about it?"

Cricket Australia is yet to indicate a desire to re-open the investigation into the events at Newlands in 2018.

A statement from the governing body said: "There has been a great deal of speculation in the eight years since the 2018 Cape Town Test, including extensive media coverage throughout last month's series in South Africa.

"During this time there has been the ongoing opportunity to present any relevant information, and this remains the case. All relevant information presented to CA to date has been properly considered and we remain comfortable with the findings of our integrity process."

SportsTab.title: Reece Walsh: World Cup semi-final brings out best and worst of Australia star
SportsTab.text:
On a fractious night in Sydney, it was no surprise to see Reece Walsh at the centre of the action – for better or worse.

The full-back scored three of Australia's eight tries as they beat Samoa 44-12 to reach a 16th successive men's Rugby League World Cup final.

His two second-half tries helped keep a burgeoning Samoa comeback at bay, while his first-half effort demonstrated his skill and showmanship.

On 32 minutes, Walsh administered the harshest of punishments on Samoa for the smallest amount of defensive laxity, racing through the tiniest gap on the left to score.

In front of approximately 40,000 spectators, the Kangaroos' number one celebrated with a backflip.

It was the kind of celebration you expect from a man once christened by Australian Rugby League Commission chairman Peter V'landys as "the Justin Bieber of rugby league" and "charisma on steroids".

But while thrilling the fans, it gives kittens to those in charge. Walsh lost his boot during the flip; when sitting down to put it back on, TV commentators fretted he had injured himself.

Australia coach Kevin Walters pointedly said there would be no backflips in the second half during a half-time interview – and indeed Walsh reined himself in.

"That's just Reece," Walters told the post-match media conference. "He always brings up something you don't expect.

"The backflip was no different. Impressive though. He did it for some sick kids. They all asked him to do a backflip if he scored a try, so you can't really be against that when he's putting a smile on kids' faces."

More concerning for Walters will be the mistakes Walsh made as he got swept up in the feverish atmosphere.

Two minutes before Walsh's first try, Samoa's Stephen Crichton appeared to have grounded to close the score to 16-6 after Francis Manuleleua had beaten the Aussie full-back to a high ball.

A slow-motion replay led to the debatable conclusion Manuleleua had knocked on. Whether the correct call or not, it was a massive let-off for Walsh.

Samoa began to lose their heads soon after, with a major flashpoint coming after Walsh was ruled to have been dangerously tackled. It was Walsh himself who instigated the ruck after the incident.

Walsh quickly responded after both Samoan scores, keeping them at arm's length while scoring his first international hat-trick.

He needed to after the first one, as Crichton did get his try in the second half after Walsh dropped a bomb.

Magic and mistakes go hand in hand, which is the risk Walters has taken by preferring Walsh at full-back to James Tedesco - who was player of the match as he helped Sydney Roosters win last month's NRL Grand Final.

"That's Reece," Walters repeated when asked about the errors. "He brings great stuff to the team.

"His catching of the high ball, it's difficult and sometimes you don't get a hold of them. He didn't tonight but it's not really anything we've got too much concern with."

Victory maintains Australia's 100% record at this tournament, with 170 points scored across four matches.

Their last defeat at a World Cup was against New Zealand in the 2008 final. They have won 22 consecutive games since then, winning the past three tournaments.

To avoid a repeat of 2008 when the meet the Kiwis in Brisbane next Sunday, they will need Walsh at his best to deal with the returned Kalyn Ponga.

New Zealand full-back Ponga, who battled on for 20 minutes with a broken arm in their thrilling 24-22 opening game defeat by Australia, remarkably returned for the semi-final against Tonga on Saturday and produced a man-of-the-match display.

In that opener back on 15 October, Walsh delivered a superb try-saving tackle on opposite number Ponga during the first half before scoring with a sensational 60-metre burst to lay the platform for the Kangaroos' last-gasp victory.

That was despite the fact that, in the run-up to the World Cup, Walsh had not played for eight weeks because of an ankle injury.

Afterwards he was vomiting in the changing room because of the effort, according to Walters. He may need to plunge those depths again.

"We all know Kalyn," said Walters. "He's a world-class player; he showed that last night.

"For the players, it's been about what we can do as a team. If we get that right, I'm happy with that."

For Samoa, a second successive World Cup ends in defeat by Australia, after being beaten 30-10 in the final four years ago.

The two nations have met six times, with Australia winning all six.

But this one hurt more. Samoa clearly felt they could win, as their ultra-aggressive Siva Tau war dance pre-match proved – getting right in the Australian faces, even forehead to forehead in some cases.

But they were aggrieved by some debatable refereeing decisions, including two disallowed tries – Crichton in the first half, then Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow denied with 10 minutes to go after contact between Manuleleua and Liam Martin was deemed illegal.

It bubbled over shortly before the break, when Spencer Leniu was sin-binned for dissent by Australian referee Adam Gee.

"You guys saw the game. You report on it," was Samoa coach Ben Gardiner's terse response to questions about the decisions.

On whether his side cost themselves with a lack of discipline, he said: "I'm not quite sure.

"On the back of some of the penalties that were given, we just didn't react very well. There was one thing into another and then a try. It made it difficult to be able to fight back from that.

"And then to be down by 18 points, 20 points at half-time, to chase back from that... I thought we did well in the second half to fight back.

"But then again, we scored a try and gave up another one straight away. We bounced off too many tackles in that early period, missed too many tackles in the game in general.

"That had nothing to do with the emotion. That's a Test match, that's what you do. It's physical, there's push and shove, stand your ground."

SportsTab.title: Marc Guehi: Manchester City defender a doubt for England camp with hip issue
SportsTab.text:
Manchester City defender Marc Guehi will undergo a scan on a hip complaint on Sunday to determine whether he can report for England duty this week.

The 26-year-old was substituted at half-time of City's loss at Nottingham Forest on Saturday and manager Enzo Maresca revealed afterwards the centre-back had requested to come off because of the injury.

Maresca did not specify Guehi's issue, but it is understood he has been troubled by the hip problem in recent weeks.

The fact he requested to be substituted has placed doubt over whether he will be available for England's Uefa Nations League matches against Croatia and Spain.

Guehi will undergo tests, although it is likely England medical staff will also want to assess the player before a final decision is made.

Thomas Tuchel will be hoping the defender is passed fit, with the former Crystal Palace captain a mainstay of his team since his appointment as England head coach in January 2025.

Guehi started in all but one of England's games at the World Cup and all four of the team's Nations League fixtures in September and October.

England face Croatia at Wembley on Thursday, 12 November, before travelling to Madrid to face World Cup winners Spain on Saturday, 15 November.

SportsTab.title: Knicks defend Taylor Swift after players name her 'fakest celebrity fan'
SportsTab.text:
The New York Knicks has defended superstar Taylor Swift, after players named her as the fakest celebrity fan.

The basketball team's point guards Tyler Kolek and Miles McBride were asked who the least genuine celebrity Knicks fan was during a NBA 2K livestream on Thursday.

"At the Knicks games, I would say it's very performative, cause like they just want to be seen at the game, they're not necessarily fans. Maybe Taylor Swift?" Kolek responded.

McBride added: "I would agree."

In May and June this year, Swift attended Game Three of the NBA Eastern Conference Finals in Cleveland and Game Four of the NBA Finals in New York City.

"I don't know if I've seen her at any other games," Kolak said.

A spokesperson for the Knicks defended Swift on Friday, telling media: "Taylor Swift has been a Knicks fan for many years, has a long history with Madison Square Garden, and we are incredibly appreciative of her support of the organisation."

The BBC has approached the Knicks for comment.

McBride added that "everybody else is usually solid", citing actor Ben Stiller and comedian Tracy Morgan as examples.

SportsTab.text:

John McGinn slams it in, and yet again United have started a half badly.

Updated at 12.39 EST

Penalty to Villa!

Dalot lunges at Alysson, who goes down – and the whistle goes. It’s unlikely to be overturned.

46 min United sub: Maguire is off, presumed injured. Ayden Heaven is on – not the more experienced Matthijs de Ligt.

On Sky, Roy Keane and Ashley Young (who played for both clubs) have been giving their views. They blame Diogo Dalot more than Senne Lammens for the Villa goals. Keane thinks United are still too open at the back, but they’ve done well since going 2-0 down. “They’ve put in the running.”

They lead on shots (12-6), shots on target (5-3) and corners (4-1).

“The League should do something about it,” says Loig Allix Van Thi. About what? “Jackson’s throat-slash signature celebration is just unacceptable. End of.”

“At the stroke of halftime,” says Peter Oh, “the Telemundo broadcast I’m watching here in California showed an ad for a global fast food chain touting a new menu item called a Crunchadilla. Either my glasses aren’t on or my faith in Unai Emery is at a low ebb because I read it as Crunchdavilla.”

HALF-TIME! Man United 2-2 Villa

That was a half of two halves. Villa roared into a ridiculously easy 2-0 lead, thanks to Alysson, Nicolas Jackson and some poor keeping from Senne Lammens. But then United started playing quite well. They got back into the game by their preferred route, a Bruno Fernandes penalty, and then Youri Tielemans made it 2-2 by scoring his first goal for his new team, against his old one.

It’s been mad. It’s been Manchester United.

45+3 min Has Fernandes conceded a pen here? No – it was a high boot, and Alysson went down in a heap, but the VAR cleared it swiftly.

45+2 min Big chance for Villa! Goretzka sends a through ball to Alysson, whose neat dink over Lammens goes just wide.

Updated at 12.18 EST

45+1 min There will be three added minutes after this one.

GOAL! Man United 2-2 Villa (Tielemans 44)

A left-foot thump, a first goal for United for Tielemans, and United are out of jail for now!

Updated at 12.30 EST

43 min Chance for Amad! Villa lose the ball playing out and Amad’s shot is well saved by Suzuki, when it should be nestling in the far corner. But then …

42 min Yoro makes not one neat interception but two, turning defence into attack, but nothing comes of either. The camera finds Robin van Persie, looking distinguished.

40 min McGinn’s chip finds the head of Pau Torres, but he sends the ball over the bar.

38 min Manzambi wins a free kick on the corner of the box as Mazraoui makes a clumsy challenge.

35 min Tielemans, who is coming into the game, wins a couple of duels against his old mates. A moment later he plays a crisp pass to Amad, whose shot from the right goes skimming past the far post.

33 min A caption informs us about United’s home record against Villa in the league since 1956. Won 43, lost three. They’ll be doing well if they keep that going.

TechnologyTab.title: Could the US midterms put a pin in the AI bubble?
TechnologyTab.text:
Is the artificial intelligence (AI) gold rush coming to an end, or is this simply a reality check?

That's the question which is hanging over investors, and which has prompted steep falls on the world's stock markets.

The sell-off in the US on Thursday was most dramatic on the Nasdaq, home to tech industry titans such as Alphabet, Nvidia, Meta and Apple.

It followed sweeping gains by the Democrats in this week's midterm elections in the US, which have given the party full control of Congress.

A number of leading Democrats campaigned against the unhindered expansion of data centres, which have underpinned the growth of artificial intelligence.

Fears this will lead to more regulation of AI appear to have concerned investors. But worries about the industry's prospects have been growing for some time.

The release of Chat GPT by Open AI in late 2022 is widely seen as having generated massive public and corporate interest in the practical uses of AI. It also sparked a modern-day gold rush.

Investors flocked to put their money into companies producing computer chips and networking infrastructure, building data centres and providing the energy to power them, as well as developing the AI itself. The value of tech companies soared.

The boom continued into this year. Investments in AI are expected to reach $1trillion in 2026 alone according to research by Goldman Sachs. The sector has scooped up so much available cash that other industries have seen their own borrowing costs increase as a result.

But investors want returns, and in recent months concerns have been growing about whether the AI boom can produce the expected riches.

Those worries have emerged at a time when public comments from AI researchers casting doubt over the safety of artificial intelligence - even suggesting it could represent an existential threat to humanity - have been grabbing headlines and fuelling speculation that a clampdown could lie ahead.

While the Trump administration has been all-in on AI, or "super intelligence" as the president likes to call it, many leading Democrats tapped into grassroots concerns about the expansion of data centres and their impact on local communities.

These were largely focused on the facilities' high consumption of water and electricity, which many feared would push up their household bills – as well as the noise, use of land, and general disruption associated with them.

A Gallup poll published in May showed 71% of Americans would oppose the building of a data centre in their community. The figure for a nuclear power station was 53%.

James Talarico, who won the Senate race in once staunchly Republican Texas, was one of those to respond to this scepticism.

"While we want to protect America's leadership in artificial intelligence, we are still grappling with how it will affect everything from how we work to how our children learn," he said.

"We must protect Americans and establish clear, consistent laws for businesses."

With control of both houses of Congress, Democrats are now expected to challenge the president's technology agenda more vigorously, while introducing legislation which could curb the expansion of the industry.

Texas' Democratic governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned against data centres, pledging a moratorium on the construction of new facilities.

Hinojosa's win could present opposition to tech multi-billionaire Elon Musk, who has moved large parts of SpaceX and Tesla's operations to the state, for years a Republican stronghold.

The Tesla boss had spent nearly $450m to back Republican campaigns in the midterms.

As the co-founder of the British-based technology firm Arm Holdings, Tudor Brown, points out, "stock values are based on future earnings not present earnings". If the rewards are not likely to be as great as expected, some investors will choose to sell up.

The falls seen on stock markets over the past 24 hours would appear to have been triggered by the midterm results. But concerns that tech firms have become overvalued were being expressed long before the elections.

The question now is whether this is simply the removal of froth from an over-exuberant market, or a sign that the AI rush is a bubble about to burst, with much wider consequences.

Nandini Roy Choudhury of Future Market Insights thinks investors will assess whether the political shift could result in restrictions on data centre construction, energy consumption and the deployment of AI technology.

She adds there is unlikely to be an immediate widespread recovery in tech stocks as traders are likely to be more selective, favouring firms with stronger balance sheets.

Brown thinks the impact will be limited. Share valuations, he thinks, were inflated by expectations of "almost infinite AI growth", which have been followed by "a bit of a panic".

"There is a natural floor to this", he says. "After that it will reflect I think that actually there's still a lot of money being made in these companies".

TechnologyTab.title: Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck
TechnologyTab.text:
Tesla will wind down production of its Cybertruck vehicles at its Texas factory next year, Elon Musk says.

He did not spell out whether it plans to stop making them entirely or shift production elsewhere, but did say the decision was to "make room" for building more of its self-driving Cybercab cars.

But the project's lead engineer, Wes Morrill, appeared to suggest the vehicle was being discontinued, writing on X: "Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab."

With its distinctive angular looks, the Cybertruck attracted diehard fans, but was beset by delays before being launched in 2023 and has had disappointing sales numbers since.

Tesla fans have been mourning the news online, with one person calling it "the best vehicle Tesla has ever made, external" as he lamented it being "discontinued next year".

Musk responded to the user, external with the word "true", adding: "But the Cybertruck fleet will be around for a long time."

Tesla's stock rose 4.7% on Friday after his announcement.

The vehicle has always been a passion project for Musk. He said it was "way more awesome than people realise, external" in March, and called it the "best product Tesla has ever made to date, external" in April.

But there have always been big questions about whether consumers shared that view and whether the Cybertruck could cut through and earn a spot in the US' lucrative truck market.

It was not helped by inauspicious introduction to the public in 2019 when Musk attempted to show off the Cybertruck's apparently unbreakable glass, only for it to shatter during a live demonstration.

TechnologyTab.title: Ocarina of Time review: Does Nintendo's Zelda remake match its original?
TechnologyTab.text:
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time was finally released on Thursday, after years of rumours that Nintendo would remake the game - considered one of the best ever made.

IGN called it "the biggest game of the decade" in their review, external when it launched in 1998 on the N64, and it set the standard for 3D games.

A lot of the things we take for granted in modern games - such as riding a horse, fighting with a sword and shield, or locking on to enemies with the tap of a button - were pioneered or perfected in Ocarina of Time.

It received an almost perfect score from critics and, decades on, remains the highest-rated game in history on Metacritic, which aggregates reviews.

So how do you remake what many consider a masterpiece?

Those like me who grew up playing the original will feel right at home here.

Nintendo has decided against reinventing the wheel, instead producing something which plays very similarly to the N64 classic.

As I've said before, video game remakes are a bit different to film or TV - gaming fans often clamour for a new take on their favourites, hoping developers harness evolution in tech to make them fresh.

And games have come a long way in the almost 30 years since the original Ocarina of Time came out.

"When you compare the games in the past and the games in modern times, so to speak, the norms of what people expect from a game have evolved naturally," Nintendo producer Hidemaro Fujibayashi told me.

"In the past, games where the users may have needed more imagination to fill the blanks or the gaps are now clearly expressed through the graphics that they see on the screen."

But fancy graphics have come at a price - a pivot away from realism into something a bit more cartoonish. Some might even be disappointed by this, given the N64 game had quite horrifying elements in places.

One was the Skulltula House, a room where people had been morphed into human-spider hybrids.

"Back when we created the original Ocarina of Time, the means to convey or express ideas was limited compared with what we have now," series producer Eiji Aonuma - who worked on the original game - said.

"With regard to even the so-called scary elements, we strove to add a touch of the comical."

But he told the BBC that enhanced graphics and lighting capabilities unintentionally exaggerated the already-spooky Skulltula House and its potential to strike fear into players.

"When we carried out the test play, the testers were telling us, 'Oh, this is too scary'," he said. "So of course, in the end product, we've made the necessary adjustments so that we can retain the same balance that we had achieved in the original."

I spoke to a few YouTubers about the upcoming game to get their thoughts - and the response was overwhelmingly positive.

Mike Channell, co-editor of the YouTube channel Outside Xbox, said he believed the remake had been made "very meticulously" in the hopes of living up to fan expectations.

"Having played the game, it's clear that serious thought has gone into every decision, to the point where I'm not convinced this remake has taken any less time and effort than an all-new Zelda game," he said.

"Ocarina of Time is obviously one of the great video game experiences in the history of the medium, but I have no doubt this new version will be the best way to experience this story.

"It's fleshed out as a world, sumptuously detailed, and the controls match 21st-Century expectations."

Ed King, known as Zeltik to his 893,000 followers on YouTube, said "the level of detail and charm" in the Ocarina of Time remake stood out.

"The Forest Temple has always been my favourite Zelda dungeon: a mysterious, haunted mansion in the deep woods, a lost work of man slowly being reclaimed by nature," he said. "The remake really leans into the surreal, uncanny nature of the original dungeon."

And fellow YouTuber StrawHatMidas said it was the "perfect" way to "bring this classic back".

"Not only does the game pay homage to the Nintendo 64 original, but it also expands on the things that made it so memorable," he said. "Everything from the world and atmosphere to the controls and soundtrack feels like a love letter to the classic Zelda formula."

Nintendo has made some big changes, not least to the Water Temple - a dungeon about two thirds into the game.

Aonuma said, having worked on the original, this was what he personally wanted to change most due to its reputation for being "very, very difficult".

He said there was now "a greater facility in tackling" the dungeon, as players can now easily change a critical in-game item known as heavy boots and have "the ability to leverage the camera orientation".

I grew up playing Zelda on the N64, which pioneered the joystick - but nowadays two sticks is the standard, with one to move and one to control the camera.

As far as I'm concerned, being able to freely move the camera this time round was a significant improvement.

At times, the trip down memory lane was captivating. I knew where to go and what to do, thanks to a kind of muscle memory. However, on occasion that took away from the experience - with some tasks achieved too easily and some puzzles too quickly because I recalled their solutions.

Some people will love how similar it is, but I have to wonder if Nintendo has played things a bit too safe.

I don't think the developers see it that way.

"Even if the game may look different, we've maintained the essence that the original developers wanted to and hopefully conveyed through the original Ocarina of Time," Fujibayashi said.

Don't get me wrong - the game has lots of changes and surprises, and I won't spoil them, but I wish there had been more.

Then again, perhaps the best games leave you wanting more.

Or as Mike put it: "I loved the original as much as the next person, but I don't think I'll be going back to it."

Fans will no doubt wonder whether this is it, or if there will be more Zelda on the horizon. With the franchise's first movie coming next year, there's certainly more to come in the short term.

And in the long term, I wondered if with 30 more years of technological advancements, Nintendo might consider remaking the game once again.

"I will be long retired," Aonuma said, with a laugh.
