articles.title: Could the US midterms put a pin in the AI bubble?
articles.text:
Is the artificial intelligence (AI) gold rush coming to an end, or is this simply a reality check?

That's the question which is hanging over investors, and which has prompted steep falls on the world's stock markets.

The sell-off in the US on Thursday was most dramatic on the Nasdaq, home to tech industry titans such as Alphabet, Nvidia, Meta and Apple.

It followed sweeping gains by the Democrats in this week's midterm elections in the US, which have given the party full control of Congress.

A number of leading Democrats campaigned against the unhindered expansion of data centres, which have underpinned the growth of artificial intelligence.

Fears this will lead to more regulation of AI appear to have concerned investors. But worries about the industry's prospects have been growing for some time.

The release of Chat GPT by Open AI in late 2022 is widely seen as having generated massive public and corporate interest in the practical uses of AI. It also sparked a modern-day gold rush.

Investors flocked to put their money into companies producing computer chips and networking infrastructure, building data centres and providing the energy to power them, as well as developing the AI itself. The value of tech companies soared.

The boom continued into this year. Investments in AI are expected to reach $1trillion in 2026 alone according to research by Goldman Sachs. The sector has scooped up so much available cash that other industries have seen their own borrowing costs increase as a result.

But investors want returns, and in recent months concerns have been growing about whether the AI boom can produce the expected riches.

Those worries have emerged at a time when public comments from AI researchers casting doubt over the safety of artificial intelligence - even suggesting it could represent an existential threat to humanity - have been grabbing headlines and fuelling speculation that a clampdown could lie ahead.

While the Trump administration has been all-in on AI, or "super intelligence" as the president likes to call it, many leading Democrats tapped into grassroots concerns about the expansion of data centres and their impact on local communities.

These were largely focused on the facilities' high consumption of water and electricity, which many feared would push up their household bills – as well as the noise, use of land, and general disruption associated with them.

A Gallup poll published in May showed 71% of Americans would oppose the building of a data centre in their community. The figure for a nuclear power station was 53%.

James Talarico, who won the Senate race in once staunchly Republican Texas, was one of those to respond to this scepticism.

"While we want to protect America's leadership in artificial intelligence, we are still grappling with how it will affect everything from how we work to how our children learn," he said.

"We must protect Americans and establish clear, consistent laws for businesses."

With control of both houses of Congress, Democrats are now expected to challenge the president's technology agenda more vigorously, while introducing legislation which could curb the expansion of the industry.

Texas' Democratic governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned against data centres, pledging a moratorium on the construction of new facilities.

Hinojosa's win could present opposition to tech multi-billionaire Elon Musk, who has moved large parts of SpaceX and Tesla's operations to the state, for years a Republican stronghold.

The Tesla boss had spent nearly $450m to back Republican campaigns in the midterms.

As the co-founder of the British-based technology firm Arm Holdings, Tudor Brown, points out, "stock values are based on future earnings not present earnings". If the rewards are not likely to be as great as expected, some investors will choose to sell up.

The falls seen on stock markets over the past 24 hours would appear to have been triggered by the midterm results. But concerns that tech firms have become overvalued were being expressed long before the elections.

The question now is whether this is simply the removal of froth from an over-exuberant market, or a sign that the AI rush is a bubble about to burst, with much wider consequences.

Nandini Roy Choudhury of Future Market Insights thinks investors will assess whether the political shift could result in restrictions on data centre construction, energy consumption and the deployment of AI technology.

She adds there is unlikely to be an immediate widespread recovery in tech stocks as traders are likely to be more selective, favouring firms with stronger balance sheets.

Brown thinks the impact will be limited. Share valuations, he thinks, were inflated by expectations of "almost infinite AI growth", which have been followed by "a bit of a panic".

"There is a natural floor to this", he says. "After that it will reflect I think that actually there's still a lot of money being made in these companies".

articles.title: Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck
articles.text:
Tesla will wind down production of its Cybertruck vehicles at its Texas factory next year, Elon Musk says.

He did not spell out whether it plans to stop making them entirely or shift production elsewhere, but did say the decision was to "make room" for building more of its self-driving Cybercab cars.

But the project's lead engineer, Wes Morrill, appeared to suggest the vehicle was being discontinued, writing on X: "Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab."

With its distinctive angular looks, the Cybertruck attracted diehard fans, but was beset by delays before being launched in 2023 and has had disappointing sales numbers since.

Tesla fans have been mourning the news online, with one person calling it "the best vehicle Tesla has ever made, external" as he lamented it being "discontinued next year".

Musk responded to the user, external with the word "true", adding: "But the Cybertruck fleet will be around for a long time."

Tesla's stock rose 4.7% on Friday after his announcement.

The vehicle has always been a passion project for Musk. He said it was "way more awesome than people realise, external" in March, and called it the "best product Tesla has ever made to date, external" in April.

But there have always been big questions about whether consumers shared that view and whether the Cybertruck could cut through and earn a spot in the US' lucrative truck market.

It was not helped by inauspicious introduction to the public in 2019 when Musk attempted to show off the Cybertruck's apparently unbreakable glass, only for it to shatter during a live demonstration.

articles.title: Ocarina of Time review: Does Nintendo's Zelda remake match its original?
articles.text:
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time was finally released on Thursday, after years of rumours that Nintendo would remake the game - considered one of the best ever made.

IGN called it "the biggest game of the decade" in their review, external when it launched in 1998 on the N64, and it set the standard for 3D games.

A lot of the things we take for granted in modern games - such as riding a horse, fighting with a sword and shield, or locking on to enemies with the tap of a button - were pioneered or perfected in Ocarina of Time.

It received an almost perfect score from critics and, decades on, remains the highest-rated game in history on Metacritic, which aggregates reviews.

So how do you remake what many consider a masterpiece?

Those like me who grew up playing the original will feel right at home here.

Nintendo has decided against reinventing the wheel, instead producing something which plays very similarly to the N64 classic.

As I've said before, video game remakes are a bit different to film or TV - gaming fans often clamour for a new take on their favourites, hoping developers harness evolution in tech to make them fresh.

And games have come a long way in the almost 30 years since the original Ocarina of Time came out.

"When you compare the games in the past and the games in modern times, so to speak, the norms of what people expect from a game have evolved naturally," Nintendo producer Hidemaro Fujibayashi told me.

"In the past, games where the users may have needed more imagination to fill the blanks or the gaps are now clearly expressed through the graphics that they see on the screen."

But fancy graphics have come at a price - a pivot away from realism into something a bit more cartoonish. Some might even be disappointed by this, given the N64 game had quite horrifying elements in places.

One was the Skulltula House, a room where people had been morphed into human-spider hybrids.

"Back when we created the original Ocarina of Time, the means to convey or express ideas was limited compared with what we have now," series producer Eiji Aonuma - who worked on the original game - said.

"With regard to even the so-called scary elements, we strove to add a touch of the comical."

But he told the BBC that enhanced graphics and lighting capabilities unintentionally exaggerated the already-spooky Skulltula House and its potential to strike fear into players.

"When we carried out the test play, the testers were telling us, 'Oh, this is too scary'," he said. "So of course, in the end product, we've made the necessary adjustments so that we can retain the same balance that we had achieved in the original."

I spoke to a few YouTubers about the upcoming game to get their thoughts - and the response was overwhelmingly positive.

Mike Channell, co-editor of the YouTube channel Outside Xbox, said he believed the remake had been made "very meticulously" in the hopes of living up to fan expectations.

"Having played the game, it's clear that serious thought has gone into every decision, to the point where I'm not convinced this remake has taken any less time and effort than an all-new Zelda game," he said.

"Ocarina of Time is obviously one of the great video game experiences in the history of the medium, but I have no doubt this new version will be the best way to experience this story.

"It's fleshed out as a world, sumptuously detailed, and the controls match 21st-Century expectations."

Ed King, known as Zeltik to his 893,000 followers on YouTube, said "the level of detail and charm" in the Ocarina of Time remake stood out.

"The Forest Temple has always been my favourite Zelda dungeon: a mysterious, haunted mansion in the deep woods, a lost work of man slowly being reclaimed by nature," he said. "The remake really leans into the surreal, uncanny nature of the original dungeon."

And fellow YouTuber StrawHatMidas said it was the "perfect" way to "bring this classic back".

"Not only does the game pay homage to the Nintendo 64 original, but it also expands on the things that made it so memorable," he said. "Everything from the world and atmosphere to the controls and soundtrack feels like a love letter to the classic Zelda formula."

Nintendo has made some big changes, not least to the Water Temple - a dungeon about two thirds into the game.

Aonuma said, having worked on the original, this was what he personally wanted to change most due to its reputation for being "very, very difficult".

He said there was now "a greater facility in tackling" the dungeon, as players can now easily change a critical in-game item known as heavy boots and have "the ability to leverage the camera orientation".

I grew up playing Zelda on the N64, which pioneered the joystick - but nowadays two sticks is the standard, with one to move and one to control the camera.

As far as I'm concerned, being able to freely move the camera this time round was a significant improvement.

At times, the trip down memory lane was captivating. I knew where to go and what to do, thanks to a kind of muscle memory. However, on occasion that took away from the experience - with some tasks achieved too easily and some puzzles too quickly because I recalled their solutions.

Some people will love how similar it is, but I have to wonder if Nintendo has played things a bit too safe.

I don't think the developers see it that way.

"Even if the game may look different, we've maintained the essence that the original developers wanted to and hopefully conveyed through the original Ocarina of Time," Fujibayashi said.

Don't get me wrong - the game has lots of changes and surprises, and I won't spoil them, but I wish there had been more.

Then again, perhaps the best games leave you wanting more.

Or as Mike put it: "I loved the original as much as the next person, but I don't think I'll be going back to it."

Fans will no doubt wonder whether this is it, or if there will be more Zelda on the horizon. With the franchise's first movie coming next year, there's certainly more to come in the short term.

And in the long term, I wondered if with 30 more years of technological advancements, Nintendo might consider remaking the game once again.

"I will be long retired," Aonuma said, with a laugh.

articles.title: The engine parts that 'fight the laws of the universe'
articles.text:
Every time you fly, an extraordinary feat of endurance occurs inside the aircraft's engines.

Hidden from view inside the sleek outer nacelle are hundreds of little turbine blades that can shrug off enormous mechanical stresses and temperatures exceeding 1,500C.

It is a true engineering marvel. And these hardy blades are not sculpted or cut from their material – they are grown.

During the 1960s, engineers worked out how to take a molten metal alloy, cast it into the shape of a turbine blade, and then cool it very carefully from one end to the other over a matter of hours. A single crystal or grain of metal alloy forms during this process of gradual, delicate solidification.

Like turning a cup of water into one big snowflake, of your own design, rather than a mini blizzard of many smaller snowflakes.

"It's about as complicated as manufacturing gets," says Ben Fifoot, manufacturing engineer at Rolls-Royce, which makes turbine blades in the UK. "It's a real motivator to get out of bed in the morning."

Only a handful of companies around the world can produce these single crystal turbine blades, and the process has been perfected end-to-end in just five countries, including the US and UK. Engine-makers continually vie for access to the technology.

Rolls-Royce, GE and France's Safran are among the few firms that have perfected the process.

In September, GE Aerospace announced, external it would acquire its turbine blade supplier for $11.75bn (£8.78bn). Neither company responded to BBC News' requests for comment but the move has been described as an effort to ensure supply of these critical components.

Separately, in March, Rolls-Royce said it would invest more than £19m in its Rotherham blade casting facility.

Turbine blade specialists continue to work on improving the capabilities of this little-known technology. All the while, China is desperate to prove that its engineers can produce turbine blades of the same quality as those in the West. Who will come out on top?

"Demand for [turbine blades] is huge. So few companies have managed to do it, which does give it this kind of magical aura," says Bill Sweetman, an aviation industry writer and consultant.

He suspects GE Aerospace's recent move is about securing reliability and predictability in the notoriously volatile aircraft manufacturing supply chain.

But why is the single crystal casting process, which has been around for decades now, still so specialist?

To grow one of these blades, asserts Fifoot, is to "fight the laws of the universe".

This is because each molten blade would naturally cool into a solid object consisting of many small grains of metal alloy, all jumbled together. But you don't want a crumbly sugar cube, you want a perfect diamond.

Getting a single crystal to grow into the shape of the blade instead isn't just a matter of cooling the molten version down slowly, the process also uses a bizarre trick called a pigtail.

The pigtail is a small spiral at one end of the blade. Fifoot says that, at the beginning of the cooling process, this spiral "chokes" the flow of solidifying crystals so that just one takes over. A bit like a hairpin corner in an F1 race right before the finish line – one driver can take the lead here and go on to win.

"Sometimes we need to play around with the number of turns or the angles on [the pigtail] to try and get more favourable grain," adds Fifoot. Once the blade is formed, this crucial but sacrificial spiral is cut off.

Meanwhile, China hopes to become only the sixth country to master the whole technology chain for single crystal blade casting.

A report in May, external quoted one engineer at the AECC Beijing Institute of Aeronautical Materials claiming that China now had a single crystal alloy "superior to or equivalent to the second-generation single-crystal superalloys widely used in Europe and the US". It costs less to make, too, apparently.

But the West has a "huge advantage" over China given that the majority of commercial airliner production happens there, says Sweetman. Supply chains and the latest innovations are generally clustered in the West. Plus, Western manufacturers also have lengthy safety records under their belts.

China must compete on practically every aspect of aircraft manufacturing, external – by no means just on turbine blades – in order to make serious in-roads. "You can definitely see that happening but it's a long, uphill struggle," adds Sweetman.

Demand for aircraft is currently high, which is already straining various supply chains in the industry. That demand could grow higher still, suggests Withey.

During the next few years, one of the two main aircraft manufacturers, Airbus and Boeing, could launch a new short-haul plane, external, he says. Then, the other would have to follow suit in order to remain competitive.

"There'll be a bun fight," says Withey, over who gets to supply the engines and, by extension, those all-important single crystal turbine blades.

articles.title: Elon Musk's record spending on Republicans failed in fierce midterms
articles.text:
Elon Musk spent almost $450m (£334m) – more than anyone ever has in an election cycle – to back Republican political candidates in the US midterm races. It was not enough to keep Democrats from a resounding victory.

Among the most striking wins went to Democrat James Talarico, who beat Republican Ken Paxton for a US Senate seat in Texas. Musk spent at least $45m in support of Paxton, according to a BBC analysis of campaign finance data.

Other races where Musk spent millions included Arizona, Michigan, Wisconsin and Minnesota. His spending continued into Monday, records show.

By Tuesday night, Musk seemed to admit defeat, joking on X that his "election-interfering space lasers didn't work."

The loss this week of so many Republican seats may have significant implications for Musk and his businesses.

SpaceX has gained an estimated, external $10bn in new government contracts since Trump was elected to his second non-consecutive term. Several Democratic lawmakers have said the company's extensive and growing role in government and national security should be investigated, external.

SpaceX's future development of massive data centres is also facing new potential difficulties - as are the data centre developments of other tech companies.

In Georgia for instance, where SpaceX has data centre operations, the just elected Democratic governor ran in-part on limiting the rapid rise of the massive buildings, as well as the huge tax breaks tech companies usually get to build them.

A number of other politicians ran on limiting data centres and dozens of state measures to limit their development passed on Tuesday, external.

Data centres are sprawling buildings that house stacks of computing hardware. Tech and artificial intelligence (AI) companies use them to run online platforms such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Musk's X and his AI company xAI.

Musk posted to X on Tuesday that his previously floated idea to somehow build data centres in space was "looking pretty appealing right now."

Tech companies involved in AI may be in for a tougher government scrutiny and potential regulation with Democrats in power, though any legislation would need Trump's approval.

James Flintoft, head of investment solutions at AJ Bell, pointed to Musk's unsuccessful spending on Republican candidates and the scale of wins by Democrats as bringing in a "period of uncertainty for investors as they assess whether tech companies are set to face greater regulation."

Senator Ed Markey on Wednesday responded on X to a person asking if major tech industry executives would be the target of investigations, saying: "They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we'll be printing."

Tech stocks were broadly up on Wednesday morning. Yet, Musk's Tesla and SpaceX were down by 4.9% and 3.4% respectively.

By Wednesday, Musk had stopped posting to X about politics and was instead posting in praise of GrokBot, an AI chatbot produced by xAI. It was a stark contrast to the 2025 election, when Musk would post to X sometimes hundreds of times in a day about politics.

He also unpinned a post that had been saved to the top of his X profile since last week that explained his "concern" with Democratic politicians winning more midterm races.

Those concerns included the idea that the US could welcome more immigrants, make Washington DC and Puerto Rico individual states, and expand the number of justices on the Supreme Court.

Another post telling his 241 million X followers to "Vote red today!" appeared on Wednesday to have been deleted from Musk's profile.

The BBC has contacted SpaceX for comment about Musk's spending and posts.

articles.title: French blood storage impacted by freezer hacks as theories swirl about culprits
articles.text:
French authorities say that fridges used in medical facilities to store blood for donations were impacted by recent cyber-attacks by unknown hackers.

The French Blood Establishment (EFS) said cold rooms storing blood were impacted by hackers, with temperatures set to rise - but staff intervened to protect blood supplies.

"No health impact has been identified and no loss of blood products is to be reported," the EFS said.

Up until now, only supermarkets were known to have been impacted by the hacks.

Meanwhile rumours have been circulating online about Russian hacktivist groups claiming they worked together to hack one of the systems that was used in the attacks which have affected European supermarkets.

Noname057(16) and Z-Pentest Alliance posted that they successfully hacked Danfoss which led to speculation that they were the culprits behind the freezer hacks.

But analysts now question whether or not that meant they were behind the supermarket cyber-attacks.

While Russian groups are not being ruled out, experts say Iranian hacktivists or nation state hackers - or even teenagers pulling pranks - could also be the culprits.

Cyber-security researchers at multiple firms are poring over evidence gathered from so-called "honeypots" to provide clues as to who is behind the waves of freezer hacks.

Three separate cyber-security firms have deployed fake freezer software traps to monitor how hackers attempt to use them for attacks.

In cyber-security, a "honeypot" is a digital decoy - such as a fake computer network or file - deliberately set up to look like a vulnerable target to lure and trap hackers.

By monitoring these traps, security experts can safely study an attacker's methods without putting real systems at risk.

According to activity gathered after the first wave of cyber-attacks, the second wave which hit several European countries was highly targeted.

"The fact that all these fridge freezers were hit simultaneously suggests planning and coordination," says Ryan Dewhurst from Spanish cyber-security company Previdian.

The entry point to the affected freezer software products was not difficult to exploit as they were poorly protected, with known attack methods already floating around online.

But experts like Dewhurst say the hacker or hackers had to gather the information about the devices' public IP addresses to create a target list then take time to plan which methods to use and when to execute them.

"Given the reported timing of when the devices had their temperatures increased, which seems to have been overnight for maximum damage - this is further evidence that the attack was planned and co-ordinated," he said.

Another cyber firm which has deployed similar honeypot tech to lure the hackers into revealing their tactics is Strathclyde-based Lupovis.

It had honeypots which appeared to be located around the world, and started seeing activity 10 days before the second wave of cyber-attacks.

Intriguingly, the team saw hackers scanning and probing their fake freezer sites only in Europe.

"We saw none of our honeypots in places like Africa or South America targeted at all," said Lupovis founder Dr Xavier Bellekens.

"Even pots in Ukraine were left alone."

articles.title: Graduates jobs: More work with AI but what else?
articles.text:
Recent university graduate Lotte Underwood is a public relations executive with a twist - she spends more time using AI than actually doing PR.

Underwood, 25, joined London-based PR agency Fight or Flight in November last year, in the new role of "AI associate" after completing a degree and then a masters in marketing.

She's part of a recently established, dedicated AI team that has built around 30 AI agents. Specific tasks include industry research, client reporting, media interview preparation, helping clients create clearer briefs, and image generation.

A big part of Underwood's job is to manage those agents, check their outputs and feed those to the team members who are dealing directly with clients and the media.

Another key responsibility of hers is to monitor how clients appear in the responses from AI tools like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and others.

"A huge part is being in client meetings and calls to work out what is actually going to be most helpful from these agents," says Underwood.

AI is seen as one of the main factors behind graduate job cuts, but companies are also creating dedicated AI-specific graduate roles like Underwood's.

Dillan Patel, for example, joined engineering software company Stride 18 months ago as an intern. A business management graduate, he was put to work developing an internal chatbot designed to capture the knowledge of a senior staff member transitioning into retirement.

Patel, 24, is now an AI automation analyst, tasked with developing further internal agents to provide specific information to individual teams, while also identifying which manual or repetitive tasks across the company could be done by AI.

"My role focuses on finding practical ways to use technology, automation, data and AI to improve how we operate," says Coventry-based Patel.

Such AI savvy graduates are also in demand from companies like ArvatoConnect, an outsourced contact centre company.

CEO Debra Maxwell says the company's usual graduate intake is on hold this year, but she plans to resume it next year with a bigger focus on AI.

"We would be looking for more AI-disruptor type roles, where you can challenge us as an organisation to think more holistically about where AI can be applied and where we could grow our business from," says London-based Maxwell.

"We see our graduates as not filling administrative roles, but actually adding value to the organisation in a different way."

Maxwell adds: "For example, one of our recent graduates is using AI to do deep dives on specific markets, and provide more information for when we're bidding [for new contracts]. It's basically giving him a more rounded role."

If AI can make a graduate job bigger and more integral to the organisation, Maxwell argues that companies can create a more loyal, engaged workforce that is able to contribute more meaningfully, much earlier.

Research from consultancy PwC found that some graduate roles are assuming more responsibilities because of AI, as it allows companies to demand more senior abilities from junior hires.

For the consultancy's 2026 AI Jobs Barometer, external, it analysed 2.4 million entry-level jobs in the US. It found that the entry-level roles most influenced by AI are now seven times more likely to require traditionally senior-level skills. These include motivational leadership, strategic decision making and team building.

Those entry-level roles with higher expectations have in fact grown 35% since 2019, PwC found, while other entry-level roles actually shrank by 10%.

Cian Clinton, who joined consultancy Valliance last September after graduating from a Bachelor of Science in 2024, says the incorporation of AI into his role makes him feel less like a graduate, and more like an equal team member. He uses around 10 AI agents daily for different tasks.

"Your ideas and your creativity are a lot more valued because you actually get to implement those firsthand, and the responsibility you take on is a lot greater because of that," says London-based Clinton, 23.

"I am now taking on responsibilities which would usually take me four or five years to get to."

His career progression, he believes, will now be faster as a result.

"AI is killing the 'pyramid' approach…progression is no longer based on your knowledge bank. Now it's more based on your critical thinking and understanding of the processes," says Clinton.

There's no doubt Underwood, Patel and Clinton are developing valuable AI knowledge which can help them across their careers.

But with their time at work so focused on AI, does it matter how much - or how little - time they're spending learning about the professional field they're supposed to be operating in?

Underwood says she'd like to still pick up the traditional PR skills her role isn't currently focused on, but is confident of her future in the agency's growing AI team.

"There's certain things that I haven't had the chance to do yet, like directly pitching to the media. I absolutely plan to do this," she says.

Graduates becoming too AI-centric is an issue for Simon Pratt, chief operating officer at Portman Finance Group. He says being able to use AI effectively is important, but the company's two-year graduate programme is fully centred on "learning the trade".

"Our graduates rotate across four areas at six-month intervals, working directly alongside senior relationship managers to learn their trade," Northampton-based Pratt explains.

"They'll learn all of our financial products, how to draft credit papers for submission to lenders, and how to build meaningful relationships with our customers. They'll progress to running transactions from start to finish."

Claire Reid, PwC UK's chief technology and innovation officer, believes graduate roles that are too AI heavy won't necessarily provide graduates long-term career progression.

"There will be no graduate job now that doesn't require a baseline of AI literacy," says Glasgow-based Reid.

"But AI skills on their own are not going to help you in your career. You've got to couple that with that sector knowledge of what that client actually wants."

Back in Coventry, Dillan Patel is confident his AI work will continue to be valuable, and he wants to keep building on it.

"I don't think I'd want to explore different positions within the business. Through my involvement in AI-related projects, I already work closely with different areas of the business and I'm gaining valuable knowledge and experience along the way," he says.

articles.title: UK also affected by cyber-attack which hit European fridges
articles.text:
Businesses in the UK's food supply chain have been impacted by the cyber-attack which hit supermarket fridges and freezers across Europe on Monday.

The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says it is aware of "a couple of instances where vulnerable technology had been exploited in the UK."

The NCSC's chief executive Dr Richard Horne told the Today programme, on BBC Radio Four, that it had "worked through the night" to alert potentially affected organisations in the UK.

The British Association of Independent Meat Suppliers (AIMS) told the BBC some of its more than 300 members had unexpectedly become what it called "collateral" as part of the hacks.

Two members saw their fridges begin to defrost, AIMS said, while another saw their cold units rise up to 100C (212F) in temperature.

AIMS spokesman Tony Goodger said the affected devices were empty at the time so no produce was lost - but urged businesses to be vigilant.

The incident "must act as a reminder to all in the food industry at whatever point in the supply chain they are that their businesses may be seen by some as targets," he said.

On Monday, supermarkets in countries including Ireland, Sweden, Estonia, and Belgium reported fridges and freezers being hiked in temperature.

The events followed attacks targeting supermarkets and food suppliers across France in early October.

Hundreds of stores were targeted by the overnight hack, which spoiled fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.

Those attacks exploited vulnerabilities in some systems used to remotely control and manage cold refrigeration units that had been surfaced by cyber-security researchers months prior.

Horne told the BBC on Tuesday that it was still "too early to say" who was behind the hacks.

But he said it pointed to an urgent need for organisations and businesses to ensure the technology underpinning a whole range of applications we use and need daily was secure and up-to-date.

"That technology base we rely on as a society has not been invested on to the extent it needs to be," Horne said, noting many firms had extended systems beyond their end of life, not upgraded them nor kept them in secure compartments disconnected from the internet.

Such actions can create vulnerabilities that many cyber-security experts say amounts to low-hanging fruit for hackers, and can be easily exploited.

But the UK's cyber chief said that they could be found and exploited more quickly and easily via "AI in the hands of our adversaries".

"We do need all organisations to look at what they rely on, to invest in renewal," he said.

"We intervene where we can. But, at the end of the day, it's your business. It's your charity. It's your life. You need to make the choice and choose wisely."

Around 40 Delhaize supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected in Monday's cyber incident, while a smaller number of shops were hit in Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.

Sabcobel, a Belgian company that manufactures some of the affected refrigerators, said the units' evaporators were switched to defrost mode, causing them to warm up.

The same method was thought to have been used in last month's incident that hit hundreds of French supermarkets.

As with that incident, many of the retailers affected on Monday said they had no choice but to throw away spoiled food - some saying this amounted to hundreds of thousands of euro in lost produce.

Mathieu Tilman, who runs a Delhaize supermarket in Belgium, told the BBC he found it "truly distressing".

"There's so many people starving, people who don't have enough to eat. How can we end up throwing away so much food?"

"In moments like these, you just feel like quitting your job."

So far, there have been little to no signs of any such impact in the UK.

But the BBC has approached major UK supermarkets for comment and asked what action, if any, they are taking to safeguard against any similar hacks attempts.

"Retailers invest heavily in their cybersecurity and are currently working with the NCSC to ensure their fridges and freezers are secure as possible against potential attacks," said Graham Wynn, assistant director of regulatory affairs at the British Retail Consortium.

Asda, Lidl, M&S, Sainsbury's and Tesco are among the retail trade association's members.

Paul Chichester, director of operations at the NCSC, said at the launch of its annual report on Tuesday it was continuing to work with and monitor UK organisations affected.

"At the moment, the impact is minimal," he added.

"We're working with organisations identifying existing vulnerabilities in the UK and trying to get those closed before somebody exploits them."

articles.title: Hot fridges, a fake nuclear alert and a $6bn heist: are we in the foothills of a hacking epidemic?
articles.text:
Alex Pearce was doing the morning rounds at his fruit and vegetable wholesale business in London on Monday last week when he noticed something odd.

The defrost light on refrigeration unit 2 was on, and the panel reading was 150C. Unit 4 was the same.

As he approached his biggest unit, its defrost light also blinked on.

It was at this point that Pearce thought: is this a cyber-attack? He walked over to the box connecting the units to the internet and yanked out the cable.

He was right.

On the same day, retailers in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Finland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden reported similar problems, with refrigerators and freezers in some shops soaring to as high as 50C (122F).

“If it had happened on a Saturday morning, when I don’t tend to be here, it could ultimately have led to a fire,” Pearce said.

But it is not just Pearce and a disparate group of retailers, as well as French blood banks, that have been suffering.

The hacking attack was one of three over a number of days. On 30 October, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, Binance, was robbed of $6.3bn (£4.7bn) in a record heist and on 1 November hackers targeted Ukraine’s emergency alert app, sending people in Kyiv a fake nuclear strike alert.

The official message after the fridge attacks is: expect more disruption. We are in the “foothills” of a new hacking landscape, the head of the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre said this week.

Referring to flaws in IT systems that are being exposed by AI technology, the NCSC boss, Richard Horne, said: “There are so many vulnerabilities out there that … you could say are waiting to be exploited.”

He added: “The most serious risk we face in the short term is just a huge rise in the volume of incidents … and I think you could probably point to the last few months and say we’ve started to see that.”

Websites around the world were temporarily taken out of service as a precaution last month when AI technology from the ChatGPT developer OpenAI helped discover a flaw in PHP, a computer language used to build much of the world wide web. French supermarket fridges were also attacked last month in what could have been a trial run for the more expansive foray this week.

To Azeem Azhar, a tech entrepreneur and commentator, the way AI models were discovering flaws that assailants could harness recalled China’s Covid ground zero. This was, he said, a “Wuhan moment”.

Azar’s assertion headlined a Substack post that also quoted the cybersecurity executive Matthew Prince, who said last month: “We’re going to have a couple of years where every single week it’s going to feel like the sky is falling.”

Not long afterwards, Pearce’s defrost lights went on.

There are two factors underpinning the NCSC warnings: geopolitics and AI. At least one expert has said the fridge attacks bear Russian hallmarks, while the Binance hack has been attributed to the North Korean state, and Russia is naturally a suspect in the Ukraine incident.

The NCSC said last week that AI-powered malicious software was “highly likely” to be used in hacking attacks against the UK’s power stations, airports and hospitals by 2028. AI would help attackers with tasks such as scouting targets, locating weaknesses in IT networks and writing malicious code, the organisation said.

But there are caveats. The NCSC’s director of operations, Paul Chichester, said the cold storage hackers “really didn’t need” to use AI to discover the fridge flaws because they were already out there, including default access passwords that were published in one fridge operating company’s manuals.

Sophos, a leading cybersecurity firm, said it had not seen any major incidents among its clients related to the PHP glitch, although – like others in the industry – it had seen a significant number of attempts to take advantage of the vulnerability.

And one expert said we had been here before. Ciaran Martin, the founding chief executive of NCSC, played down the “Wuhan moment” comparison. This was not the first time the world had faced a concerted threat, he said, pointing to the NotPetya and WannaCry cyber-attacks in 2017, which have been blamed on Russia and North Korea respectively, and a surge in ransomware attacks in 2021. North Korea, hobbled by sanctions and starved of cash, has a well-established reputation as a crypto hacker.

“It’s a bad run, but it’s not unprecedented,” Martin said. “The idea that we are having a Wuhan moment is not true. We are having one of those waves of incidents that happen every few years.”

Nonetheless, AI is exposing vulnerabilities. This is the term for a flaw in an IT system that a hacker can exploit, a door that is ajar and unnoticed or ignored by its owner. Since April, when the AI startup Anthropic released its Mythos model, which has a startling ability to flag IT flaws, the amount of vulnerabilities found by leading tech companies has soared eight-fold.

Attacks have not increased by the same volume, however. The cybersecurity expert Tal Be’ery has speculated that criminal hackers are struggling to make money from these flaws, as shown by a recent decline in revenues from ransomware attacks.

“It seems that currently the surge in vulns [vulnerabilities] does not translate to a surge in breaches,” Be’ery wrote last month.

The fridge targeting is carried out by attacking the companies that provide operating systems for commercial refrigeration units. These systems are connected to the internet, giving the hackers a remote access route to the ultimate victims. The Danish firm Danfoss, one of the affected system providers, said most of the affected equipment was old and no longer received security updates. It said it had “long recommended” customers install updates or replace obsolete software.

The NCSC, part of the GCHQ spy agency, said the hacks were a reminder of the vulnerability of everyday objects with internet access, from smart speakers to broadband routers. Ollie Whitehouse, NCSC’s chief technology officer, said this week it was “quite clear” that such devices could be “susceptible” to hackers. Manufacturers need to invest more in making their products secure and consumers need to be willing to pay more for the most robust products – and to keep updating them.

A key flaw targeted by hackers, including in the fridge attacks, is “end of life” versions of products that are no longer being produced by companies or receiving glitch-eradicating software updates.

Referring to the prospect of more attacks on internet-connected domestic devices, Whitehouse said: “To be worried, I think, is [too] strong. But we need to be more mindful, definitely.”

Pearce said he now realised his fridge monitoring system, by the US firm Copeland, which was installed in 2018, would need updating.

“Have we learned a lesson? Yes,” he said. “There is a vulnerability we probably should have been aware of, but luckily the ramifications for us were not severe.”

The need for mindfulness is heightened by the nation state threat. Criminal gangs carry out ransomware attacks, where a victim’s computer files are encrypted and assailants demand a cryptocurrency “ransom” to unlock them. But there is a cyber frontline where nation states operate too. Geopolitics, exemplified by Russia’s hybrid warfare campaign against Europe, have made this conflict grey zone a particular source of concern.

Last month, the UK government launched the Be Ready campaign, urging people to stock up on three days’ worth of food and up to nine litres of bottled water in case of a weather, cyber or other serious emergency. Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, said the country needed to prepare for the threat of “state-sponsored terrorism” targeting everyday infrastructure.

One expert said he believed the fridge attacks, for all the simplicity of the weaknesses they exploited, showed Russian traits. Xavier Bellekens, the chief executive of the cybersecurity firm Lupovis, said his startup set up “honeypot” traps involving the same fridge controllers targeted by the Europe attackers. The techniques used by the lured hackers included using internet service providers that were particularly tolerant of malicious activity – a tactic linked with previous malicious activity carried out by Russians.

“Are we certain they are Russian groups? We are not. But elements of this point in that direction,” he said.

On the frontline of the grey war, there is no shock at recent events. Experts and officials in Finland said the fridge attacks were not a surprise, but part of a pattern they had seen growing for years.

Finland shares a 1,340km (832 mile) border with Russia. Since the 2022 Ukraine invasion, cyber-attacks of all kinds have escalated. Last year, the country’s national cybersecurity centre recorded nearly 21,000 incidents – targeting a population of fewer than 6 million people. In 2022 it was about 13,000 incidents.

This year, hackers managed to compromise up to 50,000 Finnish government mobile phones; last year, they took down the website of the country’s ministry of defence.

It is a trend across Europe and Nato countries but is especially pronounced in nations that border Russia.

However, Russia was not the only reason cyber threats were increasing, said Samuli Bergström, the vice-president of WithSecure, a Helsinki-based cybersecurity company. AI was boosting attacks as well and he echoed the warnings about internet-connected appliances.

“These attackers are mostly opportunistic,” Bergström explained. “When they see something that is facing the internet, they will probably attack it. [If you have a device] connected to the internet, you have to assume that it will be attacked, sooner or later.”

Bergström and others also emphasised that Russian state actors were not the only culprits – or even, necessarily, the most sophisticated ones.

There is a vast, unseen economy of hackers in the world. Some are activists. Some are mercenaries, in it for money. A good number of them have links to states, such as Russia and Iran. But this affiliation could be loose, which makes it difficult for officials to concretely attribute a motive to a given attack.

What does this mean for Europe? The world’s cyberthreat actors are growing more sophisticated and more resourced – better able to spot vulnerabilities, more capable of exploiting them. These advances invite doomsday speculation: could an entire nation’s power grid flicker out in -mid-winter, or could commerce grind to a halt?

Finland – and most European nations – have plans in place for disrupted payment systems, or an attack on the grid. But cyberthreats are not the same as kinetic war.

Bombing a power station could take out an electricity grid for months, or even longer, given the years-long wait to buy transformers. Cyber-attacks won’t necessarily have the same effect. Software is more quickly patched; it is usually possible to disconnect a device from the internet.

The goal – at least for state actors – in mounting these cyber-attacks could be more psychological than anything, some officials said. Turning fridges into ovens, or compromising a blood bank, is dramatic; it sears itself into the memory. But those vulnerabilities are likely to now be patched. There is no guarantee that a criminal group might be able to mount that exact attack again.

Still, there are many vulnerabilities, and legacy systems, left for malevolent actors to exploit. These attacks “are more frequent, and they continue to happen”, said Bergström.

Pearce has not reattached the internet cable but said his Langridge Organic business was otherwise unaffected. He said even after the French fridge attacks last month, he did not expect his company to be next.

“Hacking for the sake of being disruptive is a strange concept to most people.”

articles.title: ‘AI clog’: UK public bodies battle onslaught of chatbot-generated complaints
articles.text:
“It started as a trickle in 2024 and now it’s an onslaught.” Hollie Wickens, a senior caseworker in a Labour MP’s office, is explaining the daily reality of dealing with surging volumes of artificial intelligence-generated correspondence.

“Half the emails we receive are some form of AI,” she says, adding that this has made requests and complaints much more complex and time-consuming to read and deal with, despite her decade of experience in the role. “It is definitely more taxing.”

At the start of this decade, applying for a job, writing a complaint or objecting to a local planning application typically required considerable effort: time to research a topic, fill in a form or write a formal-sounding email, with specialist knowledge often also required.

That was until the rapid growth of ChatGPT – which turns four later this month – Claude, Copilot, Gemini and other generative AI tools over the past couple of years. These chatbots are helping turn laypeople into experts by giving access to a free – albeit sometimes unreliable – legal adviser, administrator or personal assistant.

The developers of AI tools promised huge productivity gains for employers and their staff: dull, routine tasks could be automated and carried out far more quickly, giving the human workforce more time for creative endeavours. There are signs of those gains in parts of the economy, with AI credited for some of this year’s better than expected UK GDP growth.

However, UK businesses, local authorities, courts, schools and other public bodies are reporting being swamped by a flood of AI-generated complaints, letters and legal challenges that are massively increasing their workload, at a time of already stretched resources.

This phenomenon has been called “AI clog” by commenters.

‘Everyone’s got a free lawyer’

With the concept of low-quality “AI slop” now mainstream, organisations are sounding the alarm that their operations are being gummed up by ever greater volumes of correspondence.

These only take moments for users to create, but huge amounts of time for human employees to sift through and respond to. Bombarding public bodies with AI-generated requests has been labelled “agentic flooding” by researchers at the centre for digital governance at the Hertie School in Berlin, the Cooperative AI Foundation and GovAI.

“Every sector is experiencing very similar issues,” says Deborah Evans, the chief executive of Lawyers in Local Government (LLG), an organisation that represents 5,600 lawyers working in local authorities. “Obviously AI is a wonderful tool that enables people to do things very, very quickly and it can make a complaint sound incredibly professional, very formal.”

Local authorities are experiencing surging numbers of complaints, which can relate to issues from adult social care services to missed bin collections or objections to planning applications. “Local authorities have one pot of money and don’t get extra money because of more complaints,” Evans says.

Local authorities believe the length of correspondence is an indication that it has been artificially generated, as does the inclusion of certain phrases or use of bullet points.

“It’s a real problem,” says councillor Alessandro Georgiou, the leader of Enfield council. “More and more residents are using it to appeal decisions of the council, such as a significant uptick in parking appeals.”

The information rights watchdog, the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO), found that many public authorities received more requests in 2025. It noted that AI-generated requests can be “very long, repetitive and contain unrelated comments or misdirected demands”, have a greater scope, and be written in a way that makes it harder to identify what information is being requested.

Before the widespread use of chatbots, the average length of complaints received by local authorities was about two pages. The majority are now 10 times longer, says Evans. “You get some huge ones. The worst one I’m aware of at the moment is about 200 pages long,” she says.

Despite this, the ICO cautions that requests that appear to be drafted using AI and contain inaccuracies still need to be answered by humans.

AI tools can often treat complaints as a legal claim, Evans says. “It will start referring to statute and pull out case law, but not necessarily tied to the jurisdictional boundaries in which you operate. It might find some great case law from Canada or somewhere. [AI] is also slightly prone to hallucinations so it does occasionally make things up.”

Some business owners worry that AI’s tendency to be overly supportive and validating can give people misplaced confidence to pursue a legal case.

“Everyone’s got a free lawyer now,” complains the founder of one technology start-up. One of its former employees, who was let go on performance grounds, is challenging their dismissal through an employment tribunal, although the entrepreneur insists the process was handled correctly. “You can tell by the wording [that the complaint is AI-generated] and it has a different tone.”

Amid a long backlog of employment tribunal cases, the founder expects they will have spent £30,000 on legal fees by the time the case is heard.

The number of employment tribunal claims opened between April and June soared by 28% compared with a year earlier, representing 14,000 cases from single claimants, according to the most recent government figures. The number of concluded cases also fell during the quarter, resulting in 70,000 open single claims at the end of June.

The founder’s experience is by no means unique, according to Jim Moore, an employee relations expert at Hamilton Nash. Many of his clients are receiving correspondence that is either entirely AI-generated or relies heavily on wording from AI tools.

The complaints received by employers are described as “unnecessarily verbose” and containing “embellished or exaggerated claims that portray relatively minor incidents as major offences”.

Moore says many AI-generated complaints “miss out on the most important point of a complaint – what resolution are you looking for? Most of the time, they’re worded to sound intimidating but forget to set out what solution the complainant wants.”

The statutory response times for some requests are putting further pressure on public bodies clogged up by AI-generated correspondence.

Transport for London (TfL), the public body responsible for the capital’s public transport system, received a record 4,769 freedom of information (FoI) requests in 2025-26, a 5% increase on the previous peak in 2023-24.

The number of appeals sent to TfL is also rising, according to the minutes of a recent meeting of its audit and assurance committee. It reported a “noted increase” in appeals that appeared to be generated by AI “which often contain highly technical and often inaccurate assertions and assumptions”.

The offices of some MPs are also struggling to cope.

Vonnie Sandlan, the head of office for Graeme Downie, the Labour MP for Dunfermline and Dollar, says dealing with a surge in AI-generated requests has left her staff “exhausted”. “They are stretched to the limits and working more hours than they are paid,” she says.

She notes that AI agents could aid those who would struggle to draft correspondence without help, but says her office has recently decided to stop responding to automated “click to email your MP” campaigns, to allow them to focus on constituents’ requests.

The GMB union, which represents MPs’ office staff, has found soaring casework levels to be widespread. “AI is not lightening the load in MPs’ offices,” says Lisa Gillmore, the president of the MPs’ and peers’ staff branch. “Where offices keep their own figures, that casework has doubled or more and staff are carrying it with no let-up.”

Evans warns that every pound spent by local authorities on dealing with complaints “is a pound that’s not being spent on something else, which is why getting things under control is important”. Some ombudsman services are now imposing word limits for complaints, she says, or designing online templates to restrict how much information can be attached.

Others fear that organisations might start using AI tools to sift through AI-generated correspondence, with machine talking to machine. But this doesn’t come without cost and “losing the human touch”, as Evans puts it.

Wiltshire council has said it is exploring using AI tools to summarise long emails and draft initial responses, while a committee at Stroud district council in Gloucestershire has discussed how it uses Microsoft’s Copilot to help with writing reports and presenting information.

Researchers have also suggested authorities could attempt to stem the AI flood by making it harder for people to complete applications, by charging fees for submitting requests or blocking bots from government websites.

The UK government has issued civil servants with advice on using AI tools, including verifying facts provided, not inputting personal data and making sure humans review the work and take final decisions.

The technology journalist Jamie Bartlett has been approached by many people sharing their experiences of AI clog. “Public bodies and companies are probably going to have to use some form of AI to start filtering things out, or set stricter rules on what they’ll accept and what they won’t,” he says. “Otherwise I worry they’re going to get completely overwhelmed.”

articles.title: TikTok accused of helping to promote sex industry to girls
articles.text:
TikTok is helping to promote and normalise the sex industry, allowing “sexfluencers” to post videos aimed at marketing pornographic content they have uploaded elsewhere on sites such as OnlyFans, a report indicates.

After studying non-explicit content posted on TikTok over the course of a year by some of OnlyFans’ most popular young female performers, researchers said the women buried coded references to pornography in “girly lifestyle content” that showed them shopping, playing with their pets, baking or offering skincare advice.

While mentioning OnlyFans or directly linking to OnlyFans from TikTok accounts is prohibited, euphemisms, emojis and crude gestures are used to indicate that performers’ adult content is available for sale on other platforms. TikTok prohibits sexual solicitation, including invitations to share explicit images, but the platform distributes so-called safe-for-work material produced by popular OnlyFans performers.

The report analyses how hints about adult content are hidden in widely shared TikToks that show OnlyFans stars filming their hair and makeup routine for “get ready with me” posts – known by the acronym GRWM. Performers may use the word “corn” instead of the word “porn”, or add the corn emoji next to a star emoji, to avoid the content being blocked.

The “TikTok to OnlyFans pipeline” study was conducted by researchers from the campaigning organisations Cease (Centre to End All Sexual Exploitation) in the UK and Collective Shout in Australia. Researchers spent months scrolling through posts from a number of key “sexfluencers” and then following recommendations offered up by TikTok’s algorithm.

In viral posts, OnlyFans performers told their followers on TikTok about the money they had earned from selling sexual content. “One of the most pervasive messages across these posts is that selling sexual services on OnlyFans gives you a fabulous life – a life filled with freedom, fun, friendship and lots of money,” the report states.

Many posts promoted this message with images of cash, big houses, private jets and expensive cars, beneath headlines such as “how it feels knowing I own all of this at 23 thanks to 250,000 men”.

In some posts, OnlyFans was presented as the answer to poverty and unemployment by performers who described rag-to-riches stories. Opening an OnlyFans account was marketed as a solution, “rescuing women and girls from bleak, underprivileged lives, gifting them with the nice, luxury items that they – and their struggling families – have always deserved”, the report says.

OnlyFans’ own data indicates that its top 5,000 creators have made more than $1m each on the site since the platform launched in 2016. But the average earnings of the site’s 5 million registered performers are estimated to be about $1,000 a year, the report states.

Melinda Tankard Reist, of Collective Shout, condemned TikTok as “an industrial-scale digital pimp funnelling girls into the sex industry”. She said: “It is our view that young women and girls deserve to be protected from a predatory industry grooming them to be producers of explicit content.”

Tankard Reist said the research was commissioned in response to an awareness that OnlyFans stars such as Sophie Rain and Ari Kytsya had a huge following on TikTok among teenage girls, and concern that they were using the site to promote benefits of creating pornography.

Rain became famous with content filmed in the “Bop House”, a luxury pornography production house in Miami, which is home to a rotating group of women who sell sexual content on OnlyFans. Auditions to join the Bop House are shared on TikTok and would-be recruits respond by posting sexually suggestive dances tagging Bop House recruitment.

OnlyFans performers rely on building up their followers on TikTok and other social media platforms, so they have become adept at finding ways to make subtle nods to the presence of explicit content that is for sale elsewhere. The report focuses on the ties between TikTok and OnlyFans because TikTok has such a high proportion of young users and because it is where the careers of many on OnlyFans start out.

Many OnlyFans stars do brand promotion alongside their lifestyle content on TikTok, advertising household items such as pet food, burgers and pineapple juice, as well as sex toys and condoms. The global cosmetics brand L’Oréal last year appointed Kytsya – who refers to herself as a “mattress actress” – as a brand ambassador for Urban Decay, a makeup brand popular with teenagers and sold globally. In these advertisements, viewed millions of times on TikTok, she calls for makeup that performs well on mattresses.

The report’s authors have called for an extension of the ban that exists in many countries on showing explicitly pornographic content to under-18s so that it also includes posts that promote or are related to the sex industry.

A TikTok spokesperson said: “TikTok strictly prohibits the sharing or showing of sexual content and we use advanced technologies to enforce our community guidelines. In addition, our systems are designed to prevent age-inappropriate content from reaching teens.”

An OnlyFans spokesperson said: “OnlyFans is a platform for people aged 18 and over and we have strict onboarding processes to prevent minors accessing the platform.”

articles.title: Reform UK councillor promoted collapsed $1.9bn ‘Ponzi scheme’ HyperVerse that left victims suicidal
articles.text:
A woman who promoted a notorious cryptocurrency scam has been elected as a Reform UK councillor and now sits on the audit and risk committee of a major city council.

Susan Lawrence was one of the main UK promoters of the HyperVerse cryptocurrency scheme, which was named in US court documents as an alleged “pyramid and Ponzi scheme” that cheated investors worldwide out of a “staggering” $1.89bn (£1.41bn).

The HyperVerse scheme spread through the US and the UK from 2020 to 2022, and also targeted investors in developing countries across Asia, Africa and the Pacific before its eventual collapse left many people unable to access funds.

In some cases, people who took out bank loans to buy packages in the scheme said they felt suicidal when they were unable to withdraw their money, with some cases of self-harm.

Lawrence is now a Reform councillor on Wolverhampton city council and sits on the authority’s audit and risk committee, which independently reviews governance and risk management and oversees the financial reporting relating to a multimillion-pound budget.

Lawrence, who has not personally been accused of wrongdoing by authorities, promoted the HyperVerse scheme, or later variations of it, even after the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) issued a consumer warning that the firm may have been promoting financial services or products without the regulator’s permission.

“You should avoid dealing with this firm and beware of scams,” the FCA said in a 2021 warning.

In a 2022 presentation, Lawrence addressed members of the HyperVerse community who were concerned they could no longer access their invested funds.

Lawrence, who worked with a fraudster whose company was later forcibly shut down by the UK high court, participated in lengthy promotional videos and webinars to market the project to the public and recruit new participants.

She is also linked to various other cryptocurrency schemes that were promoted by HyperVerse’s alleged co-founder Sam Lee, an Australian bitcoin entrepreneur who moved to Dubai in 2021.

Lee was charged in the US in 2024 with both civil and criminal offences for his role in the HyperVerse schemes. He has denied all charges.

Lawrence travelled to Dubai to meet Lee, and was filmed promoting two other related investment schemes. She was also referred to as a “super leader” for one of Lee’s investment platforms called “Vidilook”. The status of a group participant is usually based on how many other people they recruit into the scheme.

Lawrence continued to promote iterations of the same network, including one that was later subject to a cease and desist order by US federal authorities which described it as a “fraudulent pyramid and Ponzi scheme”. US authorities said: “It does not sell or purport to sell any actual product and has no apparent source of revenue other than funds received from investors.”

She promoted the Ponzi schemes alongside Desmond Amey, the scams’ key UK-based promoter. The UK’s high court acted to shut down the company used by him to funnel millions of pounds into the platforms.

Lawrence did not respond when approached by the Guardian. A spokesperson for Reform UK said: “Cllr Lawrence was one of many victims of this scam, losing her pension and tens of thousands of pounds on a scheme she believed was genuine.

“She later became involved with HyperNation in an attempt to recoup the money she had lost.

“She was not employed by Des Amey and has not been questioned by any authority over her links. Cllr Lawrence has no current involvement in any of these companies or any similar schemes.”

Reform, which has been under renewed pressure over its vetting processes amid new allegations about the conduct of councillors and candidates, did not respond to a question about whether its vetting team had picked up on Lawrence’s background.

In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

articles.title: Ambika Mod: Ceiling is getting higher for South Asian actors
articles.text:
An overworked junior doctor, an aspiring writer and now a ruthless assassin.

Ambika Mod's TV credits are becoming as diverse as the roles are complex.

The actress broke through as the overwhelmed Shruti in BBC medical drama This Is Going To Hurt in 2022, and gained wide recognition for her starring role as Emma Morley in Netflix's miniseries adaptation of David Nicholls' bestselling novel One Day.

Mod, who joins the cast of Black Doves for the second season of the streamer's spy thriller, tells BBC Newsbeat she is careful about the roles she takes on.

As the daughter of Indian immigrants the 31-year-old, from Hatfield, says a "central tenet" of her work is to "change how South Asian women are seen on-screen and the characters that we are seen in".

She has previously spoken about not having access to the same "privilege", external some of her fellow actors do when it comes to roles.

Fans have questioned why she hasn't gone on to appear in as many roles as her One Day co-star Leo Woodall, who's since appeared in major films including Bridget Jones: Mad About the Boy and A24's Anthony Bourdain biopic, Tony.

Addressing this remark, Mod tells Newsbeat she thinks "there's definitely an issue in this industry with systemic racism".

"I think it is really hard for South Asian actors to really push through.

"I feel like the glass ceiling is always getting higher and higher and higher."

A report from the Creative Diversity Network, external suggested that representation of minority ethnic groups on and off-screen dropped slightly last year, after a few years of improvement.

And similar research from media watchdog Ofcom , externalfound people from certain backgrounds are less well-represented across the UK broadcasting industry.

It said "people from minority ethnic groups (across the industry as a whole) only account for 11% of those in senior management roles".

It also found under-representation in creative, production and on-screen roles.

Mod says she doesn't know if on-screen representation is changing, but says she "won't engage" with a role if she thinks its tokenistic or stereotypical.

"I've been very, very lucky in my career so far from very early on to play really complex, meaty roles and to have changed the narrative in many ways," she says.

"And I'm not looking to regress."

And when it comes to considering what to take on next, she says she tries to follow advice Dame Emma Thompson once gave her: "There's no such thing as a career, there's only what you do next."

"I'm always just trying to focus on what the new challenging thing is going to be, or cool people that I want to work with," she says.

"And also what's going to be fun, as well."

articles.title: Married at First Sight UK: Relief, tears and sadness - how cast reacted to Channel 4 show being axed
articles.text:
"I'm delighted and so relieved no-one else will have to go through the same again."

That's what one woman - who alleged she was raped on Married at First Sight UK - texted to me, as the news broke that the show was being cancelled.

Another woman, who also says her on-screen husband raped her, was in tears at the news. She told us she felt "great, consuming relief", but added she was "astounded" it had taken an external review for Channel 4 to finally pull the plug on the show.

Commenting on the review, she said: "Suggesting the programme could reasonably continue with the implementation of a 'safe word', 'panic button' or 'lockable bathroom with an extra bolt inside' is absolute insanity to me."

The Channel 4 show was plunged into crisis in May this year, after BBC Panorama revealed rape allegations from two female cast members on the show, while a third woman - Shona Manderson, the only woman who was identified - alleged a non-consensual sex act.

The men involved have denied all the allegations against them.

As the news emerged on Thursday morning that Married at First Sight UK - better known as MAFS UK - was being axed, my colleagues and I reached out to the three women who had contributed to our investigation.

None of them had been informed in advance of the decision to cancel the show, they said, although two had contributed to the review.

Shona Manderson told me by telephone her main feeling was relief that their voices had been heard.

"Speaking out wasn't easy, but knowing that our voices have helped bring about change makes it all worthwhile," she said.

Over the day, more MAFS UK cast members were in touch with us.

Several were pleased by the decision to scrap the series, but others said it did not go far enough and called for more accountability.

One cast member, who asked to remain anonymous, said people watching at home do not always appreciate this "isn't simply a television show" for those taking part.

"These are real people, real emotions."

Others we spoke to felt the show should have been taken off-air sooner.

They include April Banbury, who took part in the 2022 series and whose on-screen husband was subsequently arrested on suspicion of controlling and coercive behaviour. The police investigation against him was later dropped, and her partner called the allegations against him "false".

"I'm glad MAFS has been cancelled. It should have happened years ago," Banbury told us.

"We want answers, we want those responsible to be held accountable, and we want to know how this was allowed to happen in the first place,” added another cast member, who asked to remain anonymous.

He was echoed by Lia Perin, Partner at Taylor Hampton and lawyer for a number of MAFS UK participants.

“Cancelling the show may prevent future harm, but it does not resolve questions about the treatment of previous contestants,” she told the BBC.

"Channel 4 owes them answers, not simply assurances that lessons have been learned."

Others writing on social media said their experiences had been more positive, and that they were sad to see it go.

Jay Howard, from the 2023 series, external, said the show had brought her friendships and opportunities, while Marilyse Corrigan, a 2021 bride, external, said it was a chapter of her life she looked back on "with fond memories".

A number of cast members we spoke to also expressed concern for staff who had been working on the show, as well as sorrow for fans.

Lara Eyre, who appeared on the 2022 series, told me she felt we were now "on the edge of a curb on how we treat reality TV stars and safeguarding", adding it was a "real shame" for those who filmed this year's series, which will never be aired, as well as a shame for fans of the show.

"I know a lot of people loved it, I loved it," she said.

“Yes, I know it was traumatic, for sure, and there was a lot of bad things that went with the good. But it was a big part of a lot of people's lives, so it's sad it's not going to be on any more, but I also think this could've been avoided."

It said the review found that in Channel 4 and production company CPL's handling of the issues raised at the time, there was no breach of Ofcom’s broadcasting code.

Channel 4 bosses are due to appear in front of the Digital, Culture, Media and Sport committee on 17 November, so we may hear more then.

Either way, this is not the end of the story. There is an ongoing Ofcom investigation into the show - and in June, a male cast member was arrested on suspicion of rape.

The decision to scrap MAFS UK will also inevitably raise questions about what happens with the wider Married at First Sight format.

If one broadcaster says the show has “run its course,” then those global versions may also come under the spotlight.

Channel 4 has already said it will not be showing international editions like MAFS Australia again.

And for the TV industry more broadly, questions will once again be asked about reality TV - and whether shows like this can ever keep their contributors safe.

If you have more information about this story, you can reach Noor by email at noor.nanji@bbc.co.uk

articles.title: Monty Don bids 'final goodbye' to Gardeners' World after two decades
articles.text:
TV horticulturalist Monty Don thanked viewers and his furry friend Ned the dog while presenting his final episode of Gardeners' World, after more than two decades on air.

The head gardener on the long-running BBC TV series signed off from Longmeadow garden, where the show has been based for 16 years, on Friday.

"From myself, Ned, and Longmeadow it's the final goodbye," he said on the programme, adding it had been "a privilege and pleasure" to share his garden experiences with so many people.

During the episode, Don, 71, confirmed he would remain part of the presenting line-up for next year's Royal Horticultural Society (RHS) Chelsea Flower Show.

He added he will feature in two winter specials, expected to air between now and Christmas.

One celebratory episode will see him reflect on his years presenting the series and the changes he has seen at Longmeadow, external, which is also the garden of his private home, which he and his wife Sarah bought in 1991.

Don replaced Alan Titchmarsh on the show in 2003, at his predecessor's request.

"I first began presenting Gardeners' World 23 years ago at Berryfields, and we came here to Longmeadow 16 years ago - in that time, things have changed," he recalled, on Friday's farewell.

"The garden has grown, Nigel has been and gone, and Nellie and Patty [his previous dogs], but there has been one constant factor, and that has been the incredible privilege and pleasure of sharing my garden and my gardening life with you here, as well as working with so many superb people.

"So, thank you. Thank you for coming on that journey with me and good luck with your own gardens in the future. So, for the last time... goodbye."

The head gardener on the long-running BBC TV series signed off from Longmeadow garden, where the show has been based for 16 years, on Friday....
